articles.title: Return of the Vision
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: On Mars, former Federal President Jasmina Halsey collapses during a speech after experiencing a warning from the Caretakers about something wrong in witch-space. Felicia Winters grants her leave to investigate discreetly. Imperial Ambassador Cuthrick Delaney suggests consulting Dr Reuben Hale at the Tionisla Historical Society, noting anomalous subsonic recordings from the auditorium. The group arranges covert diplomatic passage to Tionisla under humanitarian cover.
articles.player_impact: Halsey's investigation into witch-space anomalies sets in motion events that would intersect with the Distant Worlds 3 expedition's deeper discoveries about hyperspace and ancient networks.
articles.modern_impact: The chapter reconnects Halsey's historic encounters with the Caretakers to contemporary events, suggesting that witch-space itself is undergoing changes with potential consequences for all FTL travel and interstellar civilization.
articles.body_full:
Sol, Mars, 3311 AD

The lights of the auditorium were a soft Martian amber, the sort chosen to flatter skin tones, hide wrinkles and disguise fatigue. Jasmina Halsey steadied herself at the lectern, one hand on the frosted glass, the other closing around the edge of her commtab. She had delivered harder addresses in harsher rooms. This one should have been easy: a few measured remarks about cooperative research, a nod to Alliance liaison, polite applause, then biscuits and strong coffee.

The first wobble came in the second paragraph. Not in her voice — in her mind.

A pressure, as intimate as breath but coming from everywhere at once, passed through the floor into her bones. It was almost music, a low mechanical throb just below hearing, as if the hall’s ventilation had learned to count and then forgotten how. The text on her commtab blurred; her mouth raced to keep pace with a sentence that had become unintelligible. Someone in the front row frowned. Someone else stood.

“—to recognise that what unites our—”

The pressure increased. The world tilted. Stars, a strange tone, a sense of urgency. Witch-space? Witch-space!

The last thing she remembered was the glass rim of a water tumbler, ringing like a struck crystal as she fell, the droplets hanging in slow motion.

---
White light, then soft dark. Headache. A slow return through layers of sound: a medevac’s inertial hum, a stretcher’s rattle. Her sister? Yes — Azalea’s voice pitched low and furious at a nurse who deserved neither. Smells arranged themselves — antiseptic, warm steel, the faint tang of recycled air cooled too fast.

“Jas? Jas!” Azalea’s hand enclosed hers. “You’re in Olympus Village Medical. You gave us a fright.”

Jasmina opened her eyes. Her sister’s face swam into focus, framed by the discreet logo of the facility on the glass partition. A Federal Navy duty officer glanced in from the corridor and tactfully withdrew.

“How long?” Jasmina asked.

“Hours,” Azalea said. “Not days. They say your vitals stabilised in transit.”

A physician appeared with the practiced quiet of people who belong in ICUs. “Madam. Dr Leto — neurology. The scan shows no stroke, no embolism, nothing catastrophic. Temporary hypotension and syncope, exacerbated by stress. No need to worry.”

Behind the doctor’s words the pulse had returned, a strange tone, faint but insistent, lurking on the edge of hearing.

“I didn’t faint,” she said, with sudden clarity. “I was listening.”

Azalea’s hand tightened. “To what?”

Jasmina turned her head toward the ceiling, as if looking might help her hear. “A rhythm. Out of true. Witch-space… And the voices — the ones that called themselves Caretakers.”

The temperature in the room seemed to drop. Azalea’s body stiffened; her expression hardened.

The doctor pursed his lips. “You have a history of—”

“Of seeing too far,” Jasmina said gently, her voice soft and dreamy. “Yes. 3302. Gardens and horizons and songs people kindly labelled delusion. This was clearer. Not an invitation this time, but a warning.”

Azalea caught the physician’s eye. “May I have a moment alone with my sister, please?”

He withdrew. When they were alone, Jasmina closed her fingers, as if the lectern were still under her hand.

“Jas,” Azalea whispered. “Don’t do this again… please…”

“You don’t understand,” Jasmina replied. “It’s not me… it’s them.”

Azalea sighed, rubbed her forehead, then pulled up a chair and sat alongside the medical couch. “All right. What did you see?”

“I stood in a darkness that should have been empty,” Jasmina said, straining for the right words. “But I could feel a fabric under tension. There was a pulse running through it, like a jump ship’s throb slipping a cog every so often. And the Caretakers—” She paused, tasting the fear. “They were afraid. Something in witch-space is wrong. That’s what they said.”

Azalea pressed her fingers to her brow. “Are you absolutely sure? You know what happens if this all starts again. The questions… the smears… the lies…”

“I know. But this is more important than just me.”

Silence, punctuated only by the intermittent beeps of the medical tech.

“Then we treat it as real until proven otherwise,” Azalea said at last.

Jasmina chuckled. Azalea had always been the practical one.

“Anyway,” Azalea continued, “we’ve no time to debate. Felicia’s office has already called. She wants to check on you personally — she’s waiting outside. And that old fossil Delaney has just landed too.”

“Felicia Winters?” Jasmina said. “Of course. She will also want me to behave.”

“She wants you alive.”

“You’d better send her in, then.”

The partition cleared with a diplomatic chime. Two security staff took up positions just outside as Felicia Winters stepped in with the measured stride of a woman accustomed to both crisis and cameras. She dismissed the guards with a nod.

“Jasmina,” Felicia said, and the formality dropped from her voice. “You scared the hell out of a very expensive room full of very irritating people asking a lot of very good questions.”

“I’ve grown theatrical in my old age,” Jasmina managed, smiling.

“Is it…?” Felicia asked.

Azalea was already nodding.

“Felicia, I heard something. Not metaphor, not poetry. A pulse. It felt like the void itself was torn, twisted… hurting.”

Felicia considered that for a long moment. “You know I have to ask: are you certain you’re not… hallucinating?”

“It’s clearer this time,” Halsey said. “The Caretakers again — but not announcing themselves. Warning. And there was a sound. If you have the auditorium’s environmental recordings, ask an engineer to pull the subsonic. It will be there. I know it.”

Felicia exhaled through her nose. “You do realise your detractors will have a field day with this… and mine too.”

“They made a decade of the last one,” Halsey said. “I survived. You’ve done all right, too.”

Felicia’s gaze flicked to Azalea, who answered with a small, stubborn lift of her chin. “I saw the GalNet leak,” Felicia said. “Nicely worded. Patient confidentiality. Summit proceeds. Ambulances and assurances. Azalea, I see your fingerprints on the bit about the Imperial Ambassador.”

“Just protocol,” Azalea said primly. “Her medical indemnity pulls in an Embassy witness. It’s duller than it sounds.”

“Nothing about you two is ever dull,” Felicia said, some of the steel leaving her tone. She pulled a chair closer, sat so they were eye to eye. “Very well. Here’s what I can offer without feeding the trolls. I’ll grant you a private leave of absence. Off the public roster, one secure update to my office every seventy-two hours. You will not travel alone. You will not make public pronouncements without warning me first. In return, you pursue this quietly and with rigour. If there’s a real signal in there, we’ll find it. If it’s just your health talking, we’ll find that, too.”

Relief loosened Jasmina’s shoulders. “Thank you.”

Felicia’s smile was tired and genuine. “You’ve earned the right to call in a few favours. Use them well.”

A discreet buzz at the door. An aide leaned in. “Madam President? Confirmation that Ambassador Delaney has arrived. The Embassy memo describes his presence as ‘supportive and in-line with established protocol.’”

Felicia’s eyebrows rose a fraction. “The usual decorum. Fine. Keep the cameras away from the lifts and bring him up.”

The aide withdrew. Felicia stood, smoothing an imaginary crease. “So, where do you need to go, then?”

The question hung there, crisp as a Martian night.

Before Jasmina could answer, the partition chimed again. An attaché in Imperial livery appeared at the threshold, all poise and immaculate cuffs.

“Ambassador Delaney,” he announced softly.

“That was damn quick,” Felicia muttered.

Cuthrick Delaney entered with the careful dignity of a man who refused to hurry for anything short of an absolute emergency. He was older than the last time Jasmina had seen him; the years had added gravitas to the eyes and a courtier’s stoop to the shoulders. But the gaze was steady, and there was a seasoned habit in the way he took the room’s bearings: door, exits, monitors, herself and the other occupants.

“Dear Jasmina, Azalea — a delight as always,” he said, warm and accommodating. Then, with a nod to Felicia and a crisper tone: “Madam President.”

Felicia’s mouth twitched. “Ambassador. Since protocol insists upon your company, do make yourself useful.”

His smile was faint and genuine. “I shall try — though that would be a novelty.”

He drew up a third chair — not too close — and folded himself into it. “The Caretakers, I assume?”

“This time it was a warning,” Jasmina replied. “A strange tone… and a word… witch-space.”

“Mm. Not a term many use nowadays.” He glanced towards the ceiling, as though listening to a ship hum that wasn’t there. “My grandfather kept a dog-eared primer of those old spacer terms in an actual book. Imagine that… of course he never…”

“You’re not here to reminisce,” Felicia snapped. “Do you know what it means?”

“No,” Delaney said, “but perhaps I once did. It may come to me. In the meantime: if the Caretakers are pointing at something the present prefers to call ‘ancient history’, consulting an historian would seem to be the obvious solution. There’s one place where that knowledge is still maintained without being… edited to comply with the tastes of modern audiences.”

He paused, folded his arms and waited a moment until all eyes were on him. “Tionisla.”

Azalea made a small, sceptical noise. Felicia’s brows went up a millimetre. “The Tionisla Historical Society? Eccentrics and conspiracy theorists. And it’s Alliance space.”

“How inconvenient for suspicion,” Delaney returned mildly. “Yet they are the best historical society left standing. The curators are tediously incorruptible – let me assure you, we’ve tried! I’ll admit they’re mildly eccentric. Their memorialists gather more data than anyone alive. If there’s a clue to be found, that’s where I’d look first.”

Felicia folded her arms. “You’re asking me to send a former Federal president — fresh out of intensive care — into an Alliance system, on the advice of an Imperial ambassador, to consult a bunch of… eccentrics… about ancient history.”

“Admirably succinct,” Delaney said with a grin. “We know you’ve pulled the auditorium logs already; our network of…”

“Spies?” Felicia asked, with just the right amount of acid in her tone.

“Facilitators,” Cuthrick replied smoothly. “Have provided us with a copy. Your engineers will find a notch at fifteen cycles and a harmonic smear in the mid-range. They will write ‘interference’ on the report because that is what people write in reports about things that don’t have a proper explanation.”

Azalea’s eyes flicked to Felicia. “We have asked for the recording.”

Felicia didn’t look away, continuing to glare at Cuthrick. “And if the analysis matches?”

“Then the venue isn’t the only thing ringing,” Cuthrick said. “Which suggests the message was directed — at her.”

He nodded to Jasmina.

Silence settled, purposeful. Jasmina felt the old rhythm tap once at the edge of hearing. She looked at Felicia. “If there’s a thread to pull, I have to go to Tionisla.”

Felicia looked around at the group. Then she sighed, the sound of a politician deciding which lie would hurt less.

“Very well. If we do this, we do it with choreography. Medical cover, humanitarian language. The Alliance is briefed through the Office of the Prime Minister; they issue the invitation so I can pretend I’m merely acquiescing. You—” she aimed a finger at Cuthrick “—keep your banners folded. No triumphalism in my house or theirs.”

“I am very rarely triumphant nowadays,” Cuthrick said. “More’s the pity.”

Azalea cut in, practical as gravity. “We’ll need a quiet corridor out of Olympus. No cameras, no long lenses.”

Felicia nodded. “I’ll arrange a diplomatic maintenance window on the east spine. Thirty minutes. If anyone complains, we’ll call it a filter change.” She softened, just a fraction, to Jasmina. “You are not to make public statements en route. If asked, you are resting.”

“Resting will be easy enough.”

Cuthrick rose, joints protesting in the small way old joints do. “There’s a curator at the Tionisla Historical Society — Dr Reuben Hale. He is—” Cuthrick searched for the word “—unfashionably precise. He won’t try to believe you. He’ll try to measure you. That’s probably what you need.”

Felicia arched an eyebrow. “You know him?”

“I was young once, believe it or not,” Cuthrick said, “and impertinent about words like witch-space. He corrected me. I didn’t enjoy the experience, but I did learn from it.”

Jasmina smiled at the idea of Cuthrick being dressed down by… anyone.

Azalea shook her head. “I’m not thrilled about handing Jasmina to Alliance nutters…”

“You’re handing her to a man who labels things with fastidious attention to detail,” Delaney said, unruffled. “The alternatives are redacted Federal or Imperial files. Our organisations are famously good at not revealing anything useful.”

Felicia snorted. “We can agree on that at least. The federation will produce four committees and an empty binder after months of so-called research.”

“Quite,” Cuthrick said. “Tionisla it is, then.”

Felicia looked to Jasmina one last time, seeking doubt and finding none. “You’ll have the leave I promised. Seventy-two-hour updates, secure comms only. If the Alliance so much as smiles oddly, I will personally drag you back to Mars and declare you allergic to history.”

“Understood.”

Felicia extended a hand; Jasmina took it. The grip was warm, firm, and brief. “Get some sleep. Wheels up at oh-six under humanitarian routing. My office will inform Mahon’s people this is a recuperative visit at their invitation.” She eyed Cuthrick. “Ambassador, if you turn this into an Imperial photo opportunity, I will have you installed on a Martian subcommittee on air-quality standards and lose the key. Clear?”

Cuthrick bowed, just enough. “As crystal, Madam President. It would be a fate worse than death indeed.” He paused at the door. “By the way… Ask your engineers to check for a phase miscount in the recording. Today’s technicians mistake it for wear and tear. Dr Hale may have a different opinion.”

Felicia blinked, filed it away, pushed past Cuthrick and departed in a rustle of orders.

Azalea exhaled, long and low. “You do realise we’re about to start a very polite argument with half the galaxy.”

Jasmina let her head sink back into the pillow. The tone returned — tick, miss, resume — like a vast machine slipping a tooth. “Then let’s argue in the right library.”

At the threshold, Cuthrick gave her a look containing something like respect, or recognition. “Tionisla will have the answers,” he said. “And history is very good at keeping quiet while you read.”

The door sighed shut. The room shrank to glass, monitors, and soft Martian air. Azalea fussed with the blanket until Jasmina caught her hand and held it still.

“Get the recording from the summit,” Jasmina murmured. “If it sings the same note, we’re not chasing ghosts.”

Azalea nodded. “I’ll find someone who still enjoys arguing with Fourier transforms. Damn those smug Imperials!”

Jasmina closed her eyes. The rhythm waited, steady and wrong. Beyond the window, Olympus Village eased toward evening.

Tionisla, she thought. Old words, older machines, and a man who labels things properly.

articles.title: Zorgon Peterson Unveils Caspian Explorer Vessel
articles.summary: Zorgon Peterson unveiled the Caspian Explorer, a dedicated large exploration vessel with a Mk II SCO FSD offering 500% neutron boost, and invited pilots to Reorte to field-test it by gathering exobiological data.
articles.player_impact: Pilots registered at Davies High in Reorte and gathered exobiological data throughout the galaxy to field-test the Caspian Explorer during its early release.
articles.modern_impact: The Caspian Explorer's 500% neutron boost and thermal shielding for steep atmospheric entries directly address the technical challenges of exobiological survey work. Launching just weeks after Radicoida unica's discovery, Zorgon Peterson positions the Caspian as the ideal vessel for the new era of exobiological exploration — a market that explodes in 3312 with Distant Worlds 3 and further Radicoida research.
technologies: Mk II SCO-enabled frame shift drive
articles.body_full:
Zorgon Peterson has announced the limited release of the Caspian Explorer, a large vessel purpose-built for deep space and planetary exploration.
Designed from the keel up as an exploration platform, the Caspian Explorer forgoes the "jack of all trades" compromise of many large ship options. Zorgon Peterson claims the Caspian Explorer is an elite choice for deep space voyages: "a dedicated large explorer that outpaces competitors in exploration performance, manoeuvrability and planetary operations while offering jump capability to match the needs of far-reaching expeditions."
Key features setting the Caspian Explorer apart include new Mk II exploration modules, improved landing thrusters that halve gravity influence on high-G worlds, and advanced thermal shielding for faster, steeper atmospheric entries. The ship also comes with a Mk II SCO-enabled frame shift drive that increases neutron jump boosts to 500% and white dwarf boosts to 200%.
A Zorgon Peterson spokesperson said: "The Caspian Explorer was created to push the boundaries of what a large explorer can do. It is focused, refined and optimised for the role of discovery. For Commanders who make exploration their life's work, this ship will feel like it was built just for them."
To test the new Caspian's exploration capabilities, Zorgon Peterson has called for independent pilots to help gather exploration data on exobiological organisms found throughout the galaxy. All interested explorers and exobiologists should head to Reorte and register at Davies High before heading out into the black.
The Caspian Explorer is available now as an early-release purchase and will later transition to wider shipyard availability.

articles.title: Battle Rages On Across HIP 87621 Enclave
articles.summary: After two weeks of enclave fighting, Vista Genomics confirms Radicoida unica is wholly unique. Aisling Duval leads with 6 systems, Jerome Archer is eliminated, and leaked communications indicate the war will continue until one Power dominates.
articles.player_impact: Pledged and unaffiliated pilots fought across the 49-system HIP 87621 enclave in a two-week Powerplay campaign. Jerome Archer's supporters were eliminated. Contributors collected rewards from registration megaships.
articles.modern_impact: Vista Genomics' confirmation that Radicoida unica is 'wholly unique' with 'potential advancements' validates the military investment and explains the rapid escalation. The leaked prediction that war will continue until 'one Power secures dominance' foreshadows the February 3312 non-aggression pact — Powers initially believe only total victory suffices, but later realise stalemate benefits no one.
articles.body_full:
Conflict continues across the 49-system enclave surrounding HIP 87621, with military forces from all major powers showing no signs of a ceasefire after two weeks of heavy fighting.
Ernesto Rios, a freelance war correspondent for Vox Galactica, reported:
"Although the Empire appears to be the dominant force across the enclave after this initial campaign, it's becoming clear that this conflict concerns far more than territorial influence. Radicoida unica has been confirmed by Vista Genomics as a wholly unique species, with early genetic indicators suggesting potential advancements once fully understood."
"Given the scale of the mobilisation across the enclave, it is possible that certain details of its properties are known only to a select few within senior leadership circles."
Military analysts note that the strategic and tactical situation shifts daily. The first week saw aggressive offensives from all sides, placing all fortified positions at risk as few efforts were directed into defensive action. Rapid strategic adjustments soon followed, with most Powers reinforcing key footholds to avoid being overrun.
By the second week, a more balanced pattern of defensive and offensive operations had emerged, alongside rumours of temporary concords between smaller Powers against larger rivals within the enclave.
All Powers involved in the enclave battle have issued urgent calls for pledged supporters to participate, while encouraging unaffiliated pilots to align themselves to a cause.
Leaked internal communications suggest the conflict will continue until one Power secures dominance across the 49-system enclave, confirming some analyst reports that the Powers wants strategic control over HIP 87621 for themselves. Powers are now targeting each other, regardless of their superpower alignment.
According to Vox Galactica's most recent assessment by Conrad Sterling, the following three Powers currently control the largest number of systems in the opening phase:
Rank 1: Aisling Duval - 6 systems
Rank 2: Nakato Kaine - 5 systems
Rank 3: Pranav Antal/Arissa Lavigny-Duval - 3 systems
Jerome Archer has lost their foothold in the enclave and are now eliminated from contention for control of the region.
Pilots who contributed during the initial two-week phase may now collect rewards from the megaship where they registered participation.

articles.title: Sandra's Workshop Asks for Festive Gift Couriers
articles.summary: Sandra Corrs requests pilot volunteers to deliver festive gifts after a hack wiped Our Dolph's Routes delivery data, forcing pilots to scan a beacon at Frost Dock in Njambalba to recover delivery addresses.
articles.player_impact: Pilots collected festive gifts from Frost Dock in Njambalba and delivered them to children after a hack wiped Our Dolph's Routes delivery data. A beacon outside Frost Dock held delivery information acquired via scan. Small and medium pads only.
articles.modern_impact: The reference to last year's Thargoid refugee evacuation creates a narrative thread connecting the war's humanitarian crisis to peacetime community building. Sandra's Workshop has become an annual tradition humanising the pilot community beyond combat and exploration, showing how galactic events affect civilian life at the individual level.
articles.body_full:
The CEO of leading children's toy manufacturer Sandra's Workshop has once again requested help with parcel deliveries.
Sandra Corrs, the much-loved philanthropist who provides gifts to children across the core systems each year, has made similar requests in previous years. Last year, with the Thargoid invasion just beginning, her courier fleet was loaned out to help refugee evacuation efforts.
This year a different problem has emerged, as Sandra explained to Vox Galactica:
"We had Our Dolph's Routes transport fleet all prepped in advance this year, and with no Thargoids in sight, we thought we would finally have no more hiccups. Oh, how wrong we were!
This year, we've been hacked, and most of our location data for each present was wiped clean. We managed to restore the majority from a backup, but a few presents are going out that we still need help with figuring out where to deliver them."
"Even our fleet won't be able to deliver all our presents on time, given the extra work needed to track down their proper delivery points. We'll need to rely once again on kind-hearted pilots to volunteer their time and ensure we can brighten the smiles on every child on our list."
Pilots willing to help Sandra's Workshop can collect festive gifts from the Frost Dock outpost in the Njambalba system. The outpost can only provide landing pads for small- and medium-sized vessels.
A beacon outside Frost Dock holds delivery information, which can be acquired via scan.

articles.title: Caspian Explorer Trials Deemed a Resounding Success
articles.summary: Zorgon Peterson confirmed the Caspian Explorer exceeded all internal projections during two-week field trials, with CMDR BitNick contributing the most exobiological data.
articles.player_impact: Independent pilots gathered exobiological data across the galaxy using the Caspian Explorer during a two-week field trial. CMDR BitNick contributed the most data and was publicly recognised by Zorgon Peterson.
articles.modern_impact: The Caspian Explorer's validation during exobiological data collection positions it as the ship of choice for the post-war exploration boom. Its Mk II SCO FSD with enhanced neutron and white dwarf boosting directly addresses the need for extreme-range travel to newly discovered exobiological sites. By January 3312, when Distant Worlds 3 departs, the Caspian is already a proven expedition vessel.
technologies: Mk II SCO-enabled frame shift drive
articles.body_full:
Zorgon Peterson has confirmed the successful conclusion of its Caspian Explorer field trials, with pilots securing vast quantities of exobiological data.
A Zorgon Peterson press statement described the results as "exceptional across every metric relevant to long-range exploration." Engineers supervising the campaign reported that the Caspian's performance exceeded even internal projections.
Chief Marketing Officer Devin Kaneda commented:
"These trials have demonstrated that the Caspian Explorer lives up to every ambition behind its design. Pilots pushed the vessel hard, covering vast distances using the vessel's neutron and white dwarf boosting capabilities to their fullest, and landing quickly and safely on distant worlds thanks to its unique design."
"The Caspian not only endured: it excelled. I'm excited to see what new horizons can be found by these brave explorers."
Kaneda also congratulated CMDR BitNick for providing the largest number of contributions over the two-week campaign.
With the trials now concluded, Zorgon predicts that the Caspian will quickly become a key feature of humanity's next generation of long-range expeditions.
The Caspian Explorer is available for exclusive purchase initially and will transition to standard shipyard inventories at a later date.

articles.title: Echoes of GalCop
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: Jasmina Halsey visits the Tionisla Historical Society with Azalea and Ambassador Delaney. Dr Reuben Hale explains the history of witch-space from the primitive Faraway system of the 23rd century to the Quirium-powered GalCop era. He introduces the concept of "The Missing" — vessels lost in hyperspace — and presents three artefacts: a Project Caretaker procurement note, a corrupted data wafer, and a Quirium Control Unit. When Halsey touches the unit, it responds to her with the same anomalous cadence she experienced on Mars.
articles.player_impact: The discovery that GalCop-era AI (Project Caretaker) was linked to hyperspace navigation suggests that modern frameshift technology may have inherited hidden vulnerabilities from its predecessors, potentially affecting any pilot using FTL travel.
articles.modern_impact: This chapter establishes a direct connection between Halsey's visions, GalCop's lost technology, and the "Missing" vessels—suggesting that something from the pre-Federation era may still survive within witch-space itself.
articles.body_full:
Tionisla, 3311 AD

The annex smelled faintly of old metals and preservation oils. Display plinths held relics from a less cautious age: battered jump-beacons, scorched drive coils, a flight recorder whose housing had bubbled like toffee under heat. Holograms drifted above each piece, annotating manufacturers long since defunct: Cowell & MgRath, Kruger, Irrikon, Lance & Ferman — even the GalCop Standards Bureau.

Jasmina Halsey walked between them with Azalea a soft presence at her shoulder. 

Ambassador Cuthrick Delaney kept pace a few steps back, hands folded over his cane, the picture of diplomatic restraint. Public interest had surged the moment her arrival leaked; the main galleries thrummed with visitors and local press but the annex was quiet by design. A single glass wall looked out toward the Tionisla Orbital Graveyard, its glittering procession of sarcophagi sliding past on patient vectors.

Dr Reuben Hale — thin, grey-eyed, hands permanently smudged with the ghost of workshop grit — waited by a long worktable. He didn’t offer a handshake; he inclined his head, pursing his lips at the delay.

“Madam President.”

“Jasmina, please,” she said. “Titles make people stare.”

“They were staring already,” Hale replied, not unkindly. His gaze flicked to Delaney. “Ambassador.”

“Dr Hale,” Cuthrick said, with the cordiality of old sparring partners. “Still labelling things properly, I trust.”

“Someone must retain standards,” Hale murmured. He gestured to three objects laid out beneath a sheen of stasis-film. “Before we talk about visions, we should agree on the terms of our discussion.”

Halsey glanced at Cuthrick; he returned an I told you so look.

“Ancient hyperspace physics,” Halsey said. “Witch-space if you prefer the older word. I know I do.”

Hale’s mouth twitched. “Then a brisk tour is required.”

He drew breath and launched into a rapid-fire précis, clearly recited often.

“The story begins in the twenty-third century: primitive hyperspace jump engines, high casualty rates. It took six hundred years to even partially master the technique. The first privateer vessels began explorations in the 2800s, following construction of the Faraway system.”

“Far… away?” Cuthrick asked. “Very poetic.”

“Indeed,” Hale said. “Also complex, inefficient and ruinously expensive. A lattice of monitoring satellites, branch lines, stop points and rescue stations — all built at sublight along the major routes. Hundreds of channels in the end. It took decades.”

“So… you had to travel to the destination at sublight to set up the route?” Azalea queried.

“Precisely.”

“No wonder it took decades,” Jasmina said, nodding.

“It’s from this period that your term ‘witch-space’ originates,” Hale continued. “Back then, hyperspacing ships required external help to initiate the jump. The system was… sensitive. Misconfiguration risks are listed as ‘atomic reorganisation’ and ‘time displacement’.”

“I imagine that would have quite the egregious effect on the constitution,” Cuthrick volunteered.

“Quite,” Hale said, with an irritated glare. “Unsupervised jumps were extremely dangerous. Many ships were lost. Travellers believed hyperspace was haunted — ‘the ghosts of the early ships that went into Faraway and didn’t come out again’ — hence witch-space. A large number of ships never arrived; their fate remains unknown.”

“I’m surprised anyone travelled at all,” Azalea said.

“It was a different time,” Hale allowed, a thread of nostalgia there. “More primitive but more daring.”

“And then?” Jasmina prompted.

“Technological progression made Faraway obsolete by the thirty-second century,” Hale said. “A fascinating detail: the discovery of Quirium.”

“Quirium?” Azalea asked.

“A wonder fuel,” Hale said, smiling. “Powerful, stable, contained — the foundation on which an entire superpower rose and fell. You’ve heard of GalCop of course.”

Jasmina and Azalea nodded.

“It powered everything and it revolutionised hyperspace travel,” Hale went on. “No more Faraway lattice. A modern experience we’d recognise today: crossing light-years in moments — magical.”

“But GalCop collapsed,” Azalea said. “If I remember my edu-classes correctly.”

“Yes,” Hale said, cutting a glare towards Cuthrick. “In 3174 GalCop ceased to be. You can blame our Imperial friends.”

“I’m not sure you can lay the collapse entirely at the Empire’s door,” Cuthrick replied, wryly amused.

“I could make a persuasive attempt,” Hale scowled. “Regardless, it fell — and Quirium’s secret fell with it. Lost. A tragedy. Federal and Imperial hyperspace science lagged by decades — centuries even. Weeks again to travel between systems… until very recently.”

“The frameshift drive,” Jasmina whispered.

Azalea folded her arms. “We rebuilt the ladder without the original rungs.”

“Nicely put,” Hale agreed. “And somewhere between the rungs, people fell. In the annals we call them the Missing.”

Jasmina looked up. “The Missing?”

“Our collective term for vessels that entered hyperspace throughout history and did not return,” Hale said. “For the most part it’s incomplete logs, corrupted beacons, survivor testimony that doesn’t survive peer review. You’ll find the generation ships in the list, it’s a complete menagerie of vessels in fact. And yet, occasionally there are patterns, curious anomalies…”

Jasmina shivered. “Like a faint signal from…”

“Ghosts?” Cuthrick offered, then softened it with a small smile. “Or the sort of coincidences that committees redact?”

“Residuals,” Hale corrected briskly. “Noise with structure. I’m convinced it’s some kind of signal. But we’ve never been able to isolate it. Simply not enough actual data.”

Halsey’s gaze drifted to the glass wall, to the slow ballet of the Graveyard beyond. “I heard them in my dreams long before the doctors taught me the phrase ‘auditory hallucination’. Like a pulse under everything.”

“A pulse.” Hale tapped the table. “I’ve reviewed your auditorium recording. It contains traces of the same cadence. I’m convinced it’s not a hallucination — but a fingerprint. A witch-space signature if you like.”

Azalea leaned closer. “We’ve discussed terms, Doctor. What can you tell us about the origin of this signal? What does it mean?”

“Patience,” he said. “There is more you need to know first.”

Azalea glared; Jasmina lifted a placating hand.

Hale slid aside the stasis-film. The first object was a GalCop flight ops ledger — paper, actual paper — its entries ruled in violet ink. The second was a data wafer in an archaic format. The third was a hand-sized polyhedral lump of matte ceramic and gold mesh with three recessed sockets and an inset plaque: GCConSpec — Quirium Control Unit — Mk III.

Hale touched the ledger with a reverent finger. “This first artefact. It’s a thirty-first-century procurement note which reads: Project Caretaker — budget line transfer to Standards; remit: preventative containment system for emergent machine intelligence. Status: unknown.”

“Caretaker?” Jasmina said, eyes widening. “That can’t be a coincidence!”

“I suspect not,’ Hale agreed.

“I thought only I had heard that word… seen those visions,” Jasmina added.

“It would appear,” Cuthrick said, “that someone — perhaps many someones — were familiar with this in the GalCop era. More than two hundred years ago.”

“And history has forgotten it,” Azalea said, looking at her sister. “Until they contacted you.”

“It mentions emergent machine intelligence,” Jasmina repeated with distaste. “You mean sentient AIs?”

“The wording is elliptical,” Hale said. “As you’re aware, such things were banned by treaty — but crucially not until after GalCop’s collapse.”

“GalCop were using sentient AI?” Jasmina asked, horrified.

“It’s not entirely clear,” Hale replied. “Let’s say certain programmes were renamed, relocated or… forgot themselves. But the word ‘Caretaker’ appears here and is also stamped on the reverse meta of this second artefact – the data wafer. The file is mostly corrupted. What remains suggests a supervisory intelligence capability linked to Quirium control hardware — something intended to monitor, shape or restrain behaviour at the interface between drive systems and navigation.”

“So in the absence of the Faraway system,” Azalea said, “they needed something to provide navigational expertise… and they used AI?”

Hale looked up, impressed. “I think it’s a reasonable conclusion. The Faraway system was dismantled by this point… well, mostly. Much of it was simply abandoned in the depths of space, not economical to retrieve.”

“Sentient AI,” Jasmina whispered, her gaze unfocused.

“This third artefact is a Quirium Control Unit, it was standard issue for late-GalCop witch-drives,” Hale added. “This one is inert — or should be. I’ve studied hundreds. Most are merely dead weight curiosities without the rest of their supporting componentry. We’ve never been able to figure out how they worked.”

Jasmina’s attention narrowed to the unit. The hairs lifted along her forearms; an old, unwelcome familiarity, like recognising a lullaby in static.

“May I?”

Hale hesitated, then nodded. “Of course.”

She reached out to the control unit. Her fingertips found the cool planes, the grippy little ridges where techs’ gloves once needed purchase. For a heartbeat nothing happened.

Then the room closed about her, echoing, shuddering, pulsing.

It was subtle and unmistakable: a low, mechanical throb that wasn’t sound so much as pressure, as if the deck had become a diaphragm and chosen delicately to breathe. Azalea’s eyes flicked to Hale; Cuthrick’s hand tightened on his cane. Halsey kept her palm where it was because the pulse carried a cadence she had already learned to dread — and to follow.

“Out of true,” she whispered. “One miss in every so many.”

Hale had gone very still. He didn’t move to instruments; he watched her, not the relic. “You can sense the phase,” he said softly. “We’ve caught that rhythm in the lab only once and labelled it as environmental interference — so we told ourselves.”

Jasmina released her grip on the unit. The pressure receded as if a tide had slipped under the floor and out into the station’s bones.

Azalea let out a breath she hadn’t meant to hold. “I’ll ask again… what does it mean?”

Hale’s professional detachment frayed into awe. “Madam Presi— Jasmina,” he corrected. “We catalogue phenomena. We do not normally… experience them. You spoke of voices calling themselves Caretakers. We have an internal project name that references the same, a remit about containment and a control module that recognises you. Clearly it has to be connected.”

“Recognises me?” She tasted the word. “Or recognises the thing speaking through me?”

Cuthrick’s tone was gentle. “Either answer argues for extreme caution — and for keeping a proper chain of custody.”

Hale set the wafer beside the unit. 

“GalCop was less constrained by rules and regulations. They were the first to really explore the frontier. If they coupled emergent intelligence to hyperspace, those AIs might have somehow survived. GalCop’s collapse was rapid and unstructured. Much knowledge was lost and there were rumours of AIs escaping into the darkness.”

Azalea’s brow furrowed. “You think the Caretakers are… GalCop?”

Jasmina shook her head. “No… that’s not it. But something they did — something survived them.”

Silence took the table for a beat, filled only by distant air handlers and the hush of the Graveyard beyond the glass.

Halsey looked down at the Quirium Control Unit. Ugly and utilitarian, a tool for doing dangerous things in a controlled way — a fitting reliquary for a warning from the dark. 

“So what do I do?”

“Take it on your expedition,” Hale said, surprising himself with his certainty. “It belongs with the person it answers. We’ll document the chain of custody. The Alliance will howl, the Empire will raise an eyebrow, the Federation will insist on a copy of the paper trail. Let them. I’ll keep the ledger and wafer. You take the beating heart.”

Azalea’s mouth opened to object; Halsey touched her arm and she closed it again.

“On condition,” Hale added, curator’s caution returning. “You permit instrumented access. We’ll assign a team — mixed, neutral — to observe whenever you interact with it. No one probes the unit without your consent. No one attempts to power it. If it insists on being inert, we respect that.”

“And if it insists on speaking?” Halsey asked.

“Then we listen,” Hale said. “Properly — with numbers as well as ears.”

Cuthrick cleared his throat, diplomatic velvet over iron. “For clarity: Imperial indemnity requires that I witness the transfer and that a duplicate custody log be lodged with the Embassy. No claim of ownership, Doctor — merely record-keeping in line with protocol.”

Hale’s smile was brief and genuine. “Imperial auditors never change. Governance and regulatory supervision… more paperwork.”

“It saves arguments later,” Cuthrick said. “And I fear we’re about to have a great many.”

Hale produced a case lined with non-reactive foam, set the Quirium Control Unit within and sealed it. The faintest impression of pressure brushed Halsey’s palms as the lid clicked shut.

“Jasmina,” Hale said, offering the case. “The Missing left traces in witch-space. If your Caretakers are real — whatever ‘real’ means at this point — this unit may guide you to them. GalCop tried to be careful. They also overreached. History is still being written here. Perhaps now is the time to find those witch-space ghosts and put them to rest.”

articles.title: One Year Since Humanity's Victory in Xeno War
articles.summary: One year after Titan Cocijo's destruction ended the Second Thargoid War, a memorial commentator on Mars questions whether humanity can unite without an external threat as the HIP 87621 enclave war proves old rivalries persist.
articles.player_impact: Pilots gathered at the Cocijo wreckage beacon in Sol to commemorate the war's end. Many supported rebuilding and colonisation efforts in recovering systems.
articles.modern_impact: The commentator's question — 'whether we can learn to unite without one' — becomes a thematic throughline for 3311-3312. The article explicitly frames the HIP 87621 conflict as proof that wartime unity was contingent on the Thargoid threat. This proves accurate when the February 3312 non-aggression pact excludes the Federation, and the October Accords exclude them entirely.
articles.body_full:
One year has passed since the destruction of Titan Cocijo in the Sol system brought the Second Thargoid War to an end.
The conflict cost tens of billions of lives and reshaped political, military, and economic priorities across every major civilisation. In the time since, stations and settlements once abandoned due to caustic damage have been successfully restored.
Trade routes have reopened, industries restarted, and newly colonised systems have seen communities flourish far from the scars of the war.
In Sol, visitors gathered at a beacon positioned near the wreckage site of Cocijo, a reminder of both the triumph and the sacrifice that ended the Thargoid advance.
Many still struggle with loss, while others have taken the opportunity to begin again by rebuilding and supporting colonisation efforts to expand humanity across the stars.
But the peace gained at such cost has proven fragile.
In recent weeks, the discovery of a remarkable new exobiological species, Radicoida unica, within the HIP 87621 system has triggered escalating political and military tensions. All three superpowers, and the twelve major Powers who represent them, are now engaged in a strategic battle for control over the surrounding enclave.
Political analysts have expressed concern that humanity may be repeating old mistakes. As one commentator observed at a memorial service on Mars:
"We proved we can unite against an external threat. The question is whether we can learn to do the same without one."

articles.title: Anachronisms
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: Hermine Delarue meets Cal at the DSS office in NGC 1981 Sector ZU-Y d27. The Pilots Federation has asked DSS to investigate missing deep space explorers and a lost Universal Cartographics cruiser. Cal reveals historical knowledge about the "Archer's Shadow" (Umbra Sagittarii) beyond the Core—a region once considered cursed due to hazardous navigation conditions. He mentions Hieronymus Halsey's failed Alliance expedition and connections between the Turners, GalCop's collapse, and modern ship disappearances. Delarue recruits Cal as a consultant for the expedition.
articles.player_impact: The disappearance of multiple explorer vessels and a Universal Cartographics cruiser in deep space suggests that standard navigation technology is failing in certain regions, potentially endangering any pilot traveling beyond the Core.
articles.modern_impact: This chapter connects historical deep space hazards with contemporary ship disappearances, suggesting that regions once deemed too dangerous for early explorers remain hazardous despite modern technology—and that the Pilots Federation may be concealing the scale of the problem.
articles.body_full:
NGC 1981 Sector ZU-Y d27, 3311 AD

She had wanted to take a day off to spend some time visiting the newest jewel of a world that had just been discovered in the Orion Cluster but a call from her ‘associate’ made sure that wasn’t an option anymore. So maybe another time…

Right now she sat in her spacious office, the Deep Space Surveys logo proudly displayed on the wall where at first a life support monitor had been. It had all been set up in a rush but that was okay. 

On her associate’s request she had invited one of his numerous contacts who now sat at the other side of the synth wood table. She had a job for him. He just needed to be motivated to accept it and that was exactly what her associate mentioned could be a problem — a test of wills so to say.

“Hermine Delarue. I work as an executive at Deep Space Surveys. Pleasure to meet you, sir.” She extended her hand over the desk, smiling her ‘let’s do business’ smile.

“Ah, Miss Delarue,” the man answered. “Finally. John speaks highly of you.”

“Who?”

He smiled gently. “Mister John then? The other ancient relic who always seems to be a bit gloomy and brooding? My size, the same grey hair, wears blue glasses?”

“Oh, you mean Mister Ermitage? Thank you, that’s reassuring. As a matter of fact he asked me to meet with you. So I trust you know each other well?”

He leaned back in the chair, apparently taking in the question. He kept smiling, but mostly to himself: “Just so, yes. We are what you may call very old friends.” 

She nodded at her still extended hand and the old man in the red and black suit carefully shook it, then withdrew again in an instant. “Charmed. You may call me Cal.”

She bowed her head slightly.

“And to what matters do I owe the invitation, Miss Delarue?”

She summoned two tumblers from an invisible drawer in her desk and reached for the bottle on her table, rich amber ‘94 Lavian Brandy. She started pouring the first glass and looked at her guest. “May I offer you one? It’s from a private selection.”

“No, thanks,” came the answer. “But please don’t let that deter you.” 

“Thank you. And truth be told, the matter is somewhat delicate,” she said while shifting uneasily in her chair. “Deep Space Surveys was approached by a group of higher ups in the Pilots Federation. They were looking for what they called experienced survey specialists with a decent track record.”

“And they came to you?”

“Thanks, charmer, but yes. We were a bit surprised as well. Although we do have a certain reputation in the business, we don’t often get inquiries from the premier league.”

“Oh, no offense to you and your little NGO,” he waved her off. “But as you say, the Pilots Federation have their trusted handlers for the matters you describe as ‘delicate’.”

“We assumed as much but after some digging it made sense to us.”

“Oh?” he quite obviously faked his surprise. “Care to elaborate?”

“Sure,” she answered. She took a sip from her tumbler and then leaned forward. “However, you need to promise me you will help with this matter first.”

“Need I?”

“Well, Mister Ermitage said you would be hesitant to provide help but should you consider it, he said you would have the opportunity to triumph in an old rivalry.” She shrugged. “Whatever that means.”

“Ha!” the old man burst out laughing. “At least you can see now John and I know each other. It is true not many things pique my interest these days and even fewer I would lend a hand to. In fact, it is the main reason your Mister Ermitage and I can be old friends. He has his ways… I had mine.’”

“Had?”

He seemed lost in thought for a moment before looking at her again: “How can I help you, Miss Delarue?”

She nodded: “Right. Over the last few weeks the Pilots Federation has collected data on an unusual number of starships failing to make contact at their scheduled destinations. Not commercial Bubble liners but deep space explorers. They also received a number of MIA reports filed by private citizens and a number of NGOs with urges to investigate further.”

“Did you ask them if they had contacted the chaps from DSSA or STAR?”

“Yes we did, and yes they did. According to the PF both organisations had no information on the missing ships and none of them had called port at their locations. Which would make it even weirder. The carrier networks out there are pretty sophisticated.”

“And why bother? As an executive of Deep Space Surveys you will be well aware that ships get lost all the time, especially the ones who are out there on their own. They all rely on their magical Field Units but most of them would struggle to tell the difference between a cohesion entangler and a classic screwdriver.”

She nodded. “Screwdrivers and privateers aside, I presume political or other influential circles may be involved. You are right, of course, the PF doesn’t consider themselves a rescue organization. I asked their representatives whether they would investigate.”

“That is interesting,” he mused, stroking his neatly trimmed chin beard. “What did they say? Oh and now I would definitely like one of your Lavian Brandys.” He pointed at the bottle.

Amused, Delarue took the bottle and the second tumbler, filled it with that glorious amber liquid, and poured herself another as well. So far, she thought, that test of wills was manageable.

“Well,” she continued. “Underneath all that polished corp gibberish, they fully realize they provide the infrastructure to keep space travel a thing but don’t usually lift a finger outside of their ‘newbie bubbles’.”

“Yes, ‘usually’,” he said while sipping on the Brandy. “But because your NGO is called Deep Space Surveys they thought to just ask you instead?”

“Not at first, no. But after some prodding as to why they approached us at all, they grudgingly conceded to Mister Ermitage that one of their state-of-the-art cartographics cruisers had gone missing, too.”

“Universal Cartographics? What an inconvenient turn of events. I am shocked!” He nonetheless chuckled. “Sideris must be fuming behind her desk. And they openly conceded that to you?”

“Like I said, only after Mister Ermitage dug a bit deeper. I don’t know how he did it and quite frankly, I don’t want to know. But he said he had called in a few favours and the Pilots Federation probably ran out of options. Our organizations are not at odds or in competition per se. It’s just that we have specialized equipment for a number of survey operations that we developed further after the construction of Explorers Anchorage.”

“Equipment that their state-of-the-art cruiser has not?” He chuckled again, this time slightly more fiendish than before.

“Don’t overthink it.” 

“No, it is just interesting,” he said, becoming all matter-of-factly again in an instant. “The Pilots Federation sits on a technological monopoly and together with their Dog Star pals they more or less dictate how space travel works. I thought with their modern firmware they are able to track a starship’s position through their fluid routers. I hear they run on entangled helium now.”

Delarue frowned. “They’ve been running on helium for 30 years?”

“See? What I said.”

“You’re an odd fellow, I have to admit. But Mister Ermitage warned me you might come across as… anachronistic. Well, warning is the wrong word. Let’s say he cautioned me that some of your answers would feel a bit… fallen out of time?”

“Did he now? That man flies a Lanner! And you are suggesting a number of exploration ships have gone missing out there without a trace and apparently with their non anachronistic firmware failing?”

“No. I don’t suggest that at all. It’s what the Pilots Federation’s reps told me. And yes, they asked me — or rather us — to investigate.”

“It is getting better and better. Where do they want you to investigate? Did they specify a region?”

“The data they provided marks most of the missing ships beyond the Core.”

He leaned back in his chair, toying with his glass of Bandy. “That is the Umbra Sagittarii,” he mused.

“Pardon me?”

“The Archer’s Shadow.” Sipping another sip, he continued: “Back in the day explorers thought the region beyond the Core was cursed. Off limits, so to say, because the thick interstellar clouds, stellar density and also the frequent energy bursts from the center made deep space navigation hazardous and unpredictable.”

“Back in the day? I’ve never heard that name before.”

“Most likely, because you weren’t born. Before the widespread release of the frameshift drive I only know of a handful of dedicated attempts to thoroughly chart these areas. The last one I know of came from the Alliance and it failed. They never heard from them again and according to their last broadcast they had barely made it beyond the Corona Australis.”

“I haven’t heard of that either.”

“Most likely, Miss Delarue, because your network of contacts ends somewhere. It was shortly after the Turners took over the Big Dipper. They were a bit shy about making it public at first, probably, because the Captain of that ill-fated expedition was a certain Hieronymus Halsey.”

“Halsey?” she asked in surprise? That name! There were a number of recent events around the current Federal Ambassador, Jasmina Halsey, but she hadn’t realised the family name ran all the way back to the infant Alliance of Independent Systems.

“The same,” Cal reinforced. “Did you know the Turners and the Halseys have a history? Captain Hieronymus Halsey was the great uncle of one of their best engineers. There had been rumors, of course,” he lectured. “People wondered back then how the Alliance was able to out-research long established powers like the Empire and the Federation. Some say it all came down to the disintegration of Galcop, the famous or infamous Galactic Cooperative. The rest they say is history…”  

Stunned, Delarue thought about the implications for a long moment. It all started to make sense — in a way. The troubling reports from Ermitage’s meeting with Ram Tah, the unannounced installation of a Galcop era sensor array on one of the Distant Worlds carriers, an expedition to the Guardian ruins, Jasmina Halsey’s recent statement on some cosmic peril, her strange trip to Tionisla; now the lost ships and Pilots Federation tech failing…

She took a deep breath: “I have to say I don’t understand half of what you’re saying but I begin to see why Mister Ermitage referred me to you. Your knowledge could prove very valuable.” 

“Miss Delarue, you have to understand I still fail to see how I can help you with this matter. The past is the past, the lost ships and their presumed locations are intriguing, the Pilots Federation apparently being in dire straits is refreshing, but what is it exactly that you want from me?”

‘Gotcha’, she thought. 

“You already answered that yourself, Cal: You seem to have deep insights about the unpredictables of space travel, especially hazards stemming from an earlier, less understood era. And you have a far reaching network of contacts. There may be things the Pilots Federation ignores, is unaware of or doesn’t tell us. Yes, they lost a top notch ship but do you really think that’s all there is to it?”

He smiled. “Ah, we are getting to the point now, are we not? Just say it then.”

She sighed: “We would be happy to have you as a consultant on shall we say ‘unannounced or unwanted involvements’.”

“Why?”

“Because we were asked by the Federal Astrocartography Department two days ago to accept a number of their vessels into the Distant Worlds flotilla. And while we are always open minded and willing to share exploration data with the galactic community, we of course also suspect it’s because they were kindly asked by the Pilots Federation to get involved.”

“What a daring suggestion.”

“Isn’t it?” she said with a wry smile. “However, the expedition needs to stay apolitical. I’m aware there are a lot of smaller squadrons on the roster, most of them unaffiliated and some of them pledged. That’s okay, we fully expected that. But the Federation ‘offering’ a number of their ships as a token of support is a new level. They want to name an envoy or a kind of liaison officer, which seems prudent and transparent…”

“...but you feel that is where your unwanted involvements could begin,” he ended the non-question.

“Precisely. Do you now see our predicament?” 

“Well, Miss Delarue,” he said, emptying the tumbler. “I am sure Mister Ermitage would agree that unwanted involvements are my specialty.”

Now it was her turn to smile: “He may have mentioned it…”, toasting him with her glass of Brandy.

articles.title: The Envoy
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: On Earth, Jasmina Halsey briefs Felicia Winters and Federal Intelligence about her findings from Tionisla. She connects Project Caretaker, BlackTech, and the Guardians' Constructs as intersecting factors in witch-space anomalies. Federal Intelligence confirms the anomalous cadence appears on multiple civilian frameshift recordings. Winters authorizes Halsey to join Distant Worlds 3 as Federation Envoy and Scientific Observer, with full telemetry capture and joint protocols with Alliance and Imperial observers.
articles.player_impact: Halsey's official participation in DW3 as a Federal Envoy means the expedition now carries inter-superpower diplomatic significance, with hidden scientific objectives that could affect all pilots traveling in deep space.
articles.modern_impact: The authorization establishes a precedent for superpower cooperation on existential threats hidden in hyperspace infrastructure, revealing that civilian expeditions can serve as cover for investigations into FTL technology vulnerabilities.
articles.body_full:
Sol, Earth, 3311 AD

Sol set behind Earth, the light fading. The exterior of Abraham Lincoln station was cast into darkness, lit only by the flash of navigation lights, advertising boards and the thousands of windows around its perimeter.

Felicia Winters had chosen a smaller briefing room than usual, a sign she wanted fewer spectators and fewer leaks. The table was polished to a diplomat’s smile. Two Federal Intelligence officers occupied the far side; one in grey with a commtab held ready, the other with the patient eyes of a man who had missed too many dinners.

Jasmina Halsey stood rather than sat. Azalea took the chair nearest the wall. A recording light winked from the ceiling, red and unblinking.

Felicia opened with grace and warning.

“You asked for Federal Intelligence present. They are. You asked for a secure line to the Embassy because of your indemnities. It is muted unless I say otherwise. This is your floor, Jasmina.”

Jasmina let the air settle. When she spoke her voice carried the steadiness of someone who had practised frightening truths until they fit in the mouth.

“Tionisla gave us names,” she said. “Not just the word in my head. Caretakers. The Missing. Project Caretaker. They align.”

The grey-suited intelligence agent cleared her throat. “With respect, former President Halsey, words align very easily.”

“Events align less so,” Jasmina said. “The auditorium recording on Mars carried a cadence that repeats in Tionisla telemetry. The Quirium Control Unit responded to contact. Dr Hale has the baselines. The signature is confirmed to be a witch-space harmonic, out of true.”

Felicia folded her hands. “So? Make your case. What have you learnt?”

Jasmina let the outline draw itself in speech.

“During the GalCop collapse, which you can date by any of a dozen calendars and blame on anyone you desire depending on your political outlook, synthetic minds crossed a threshold. Containment failed at scale. We call the legal response a ban because history prefers clean labels. The truth was messy. Programmes were renamed or mislaid. Others were destroyed. Some were not. Autonomous entities slipped the net. The people who hunted them used a shorthand in their journals. BlackTech.”

The second intelligence agent tilted his head. “An old ghost story.”

“Older than you think,” Azalea said quietly. “And not just a story.”

Jasmina continued.

“In the same era GalCop standardised witch-drives on Quirium. A marvel, a shortcut, an accelerant. But with Faraway dismantled, something had to provide navigational stewardship inside the jump substrate. Project Caretaker reads like a supervisory layer at the interface between mind and drive, pilot and machine. It monitored and restrained. It may have done more.”

The first agent flicked through a file on her commtab. “We have fragmentary references to that procurement line. No linked outcomes.”

“Because the outcomes ended with the collapse,” Jasmina said. “Law followed disaster, not reason. If Caretaker failed where BlackTech leaked into drive systems we would outlaw minds rather than admit we had built ladders across a well then danced on them.”

The second agent steepled his fingers. “You are implying a three-body problem. Synthetic entities, the Quirium drives and this — Caretaker — sat between them.”

“I am stating it,” Jasmina said. “Now add an external vector. The Guardians engineered synthetic minds of their own. Constructs designed to police, preserve, then later to fight their creators when the philosophy soured. We do not know the fate of those minds. We only know that where civilisation invests its soul in machines those machines echo beyond the fall. We still trip over their footprints.”

Felicia’s gaze narrowed, not hostile, interested. “Too poetic for my taste, Jasmina. You mentioned the Missing — who are they?”

“Vessels that entered witch-space and did not return,” Jasmina said. “In the data Hale keeps the Missing are not random. Against the hiss of noise there are faint structures. Periodic whispers. If Caretaker was a brake it was also a witness. If BlackTech learned to hide in it somehow it would use the same corridor. If the Guardians’ Constructs learned anything about us they learned it in the same dark spaces.”

The first agent’s mouth made a thin line. “This is a chain of conjectures.”

“It is,” Jasmina agreed. “But the links are strong. The pulse is real. The unit answered me. The word Caretaker appears where it should not. My visions have moved from metaphor to message. I can ignore that and await the next collapse or I can follow the pull while we still have the luxury to argue about adjectives.”

Felicia looked to the intelligence officers. “Director?”

The second agent spoke first. “We ran the Mars audio through our own stack. There is a notch and a smear in the low band we cannot attribute to ventilation or crowd noise. We found the same artefact on three civilian frameshift recordings filed as complaints about ‘odd tones’ on long hauls. Independent samples, different ships, matching cadence. The Tionisla sample is better. Dr Hale is a nuisance… but he is a competent nuisance.”

The first agent nodded, reluctantly. “We classify the pattern as anomalous, not merely aesthetic.”

Felicia turned back to Jasmina. “So… what do you want?”

Jasmina did not pretend the list was modest.

“Authority. Cover. A way to be useful that is not a podium. The Distant Worlds 3 expedition is assembling. It will go where our charts thin to sketches. Officially I go as a Federation Envoy and Scientific Observer. Morale calls, diplomatic tea, a smile for the cameras whenever they insist.” She paused. “In truth I go because the pull in my head points away from Sol. If there is a seam in witch-space that is where it has frayed. The answers are out there, not here.”

Azalea had been silent until now, but she added the practical line. “Alliance and Imperial liaisons are already threaded into the expedition. They will have eyes. Better that ours are present and authorised.”

The first agent frowned. “Risk profile is non-trivial. Health concerns remain. The last time you were caught up in visions we inherited a decade of nonsense.”

Felicia did not scold the tone. She let it hang then cut it. “The last time we also learned to tell nonsense from signal. We are not as afraid as we were then. This time there is hard evidence of… something.”

The second agent nodded. “If we authorise this we will require telemetry. Full passive capture whenever you interact with the Quirium artefact. Psychological and neurological baselines before departure and at scheduled intervals en route. A secure courier window to move data home.”

Jasmina inclined her head. “Agreed. Dr Hale’s team already drafted an instrument plan. Make it a joint protocol. Alliance and Empire can see the raw numbers on a time delay. No one gets to turn a graph into a press release before we do.”

Felicia’s mouth twitched at that. “You have not lost your taste for choreography.”

“Only my tolerance for messy dancing,” Jasmina said, with a smile.

Silence walked around the room for a moment, counting the cost of decisions. Beyond the glass a shuttle drifted like a thought that had not found words.

Felicia came to her feet. It was not theatre. It was weight.

“Very well,” she said. “You will join Distant Worlds 3 as Federation Envoy and Scientific Observer. Officially your duties are morale and diplomacy. Unofficially you will coordinate with Deep Space Surveys on calibration, with the Tionisla Historical Society on interpretation and with our own analysts on capture. You will supply a secure update every seventy-two hours. If the expedition enters regions without relay you will cache to courier. If your health wavers you return. If any superpower tries to turn this into a flag ceremony you smile then you call me.”

The first agent opened her mouth. Felicia lifted a hand. “Yes, the paperwork will be a nightmare. That’s what I pay you for. Get to it.”

Azalea breathed out. Some of the tension left her shoulders. “We will keep the envoy alive,” she said, to no one in particular.

The second agent pushed a file across the table.

“Provisional clearances. A contact list for science teams willing to work without grandstanding. A quiet supply of sensor packages loaded on independent hulls in case the expedition outruns its own logistics.”

Felicia’s gaze held Jasmina’s. “Last question. Why you? Not the politics. Not the notoriety. Why you?”

Jasmina did not look away.

“Because the pulse answers me. Because the unit answered my hand. Because the vision is not a painting any more. The Caretakers are not singing about gardens. They are whispering about a broken gear in the dark. I do not know if they are GalCop dead, BlackTech loose or something that grew out of older soil when the Guardians spoke to their machines. I only know the seam is there and that I can feel the tug.”

Felicia nodded once, a decision landing. “Then go tug back.”

She pressed her thumb to the console. The secure line to the Embassy unmuted with a soft tone. “Ambassador Delaney,” she said without looking at the camera, “you may inform your auditors that the Federation has authorised Halsey’s participation in Distant Worlds 3. Protocols will be shared. Try not to enjoy the paperwork.”

Cuthrick’s voice arrived like old velvet from a tin. “Madam President, I never enjoy paperwork. I only respect it. Godspeed to your envoy. An uncharacteristically wise decision from the Federation, I applaud it.”

Felicia rolled her eyes.

The line clicked off. Felicia rounded the table and took Jasmina’s hands. The grip was firm, then gone.

“Pack light,” she said. “Not that you will. Get your baselines done today. Your berth will be where the expedition planners say it is. I will pretend I do not know the callsign.”

Jasmina smiled. “Plausible deniability as always.”

As they turned to leave the recording light went dark. Azalea fell into step beside her, a quiet orbit. In the corridor the station’s air tasted faintly of dust and iron.

“DW3,” Azalea murmured. “We will be the dullest diplomats in history.”

“Let us hope,” Jasmina said. The pulse brushed her perception then, not a sound but a shape, one beat wrong out of many right. It came from a direction she could not point to on a map yet.

Beyond Sol, past routes the Faraway never touched, something waited in a corridor of their own making. She would follow. Officially for morale, for diplomacy. In truth for the seam. For the Missing. For the word an old ledger had carried like an ember.

Caretaker.

And I’m humanity’s envoy to them, whatever they might be.

articles.title: Third Distant Worlds Expedition Requests Materials for Deep-Space Infrastructure Project
articles.summary: The Distant Worlds working group issues a community appeal for mined and manufactured materials to construct a new deep-space facility beyond established survey routes. Executive Operative Hermine Delarue and quartermaster Timotheus Haddard outline the initial requirements, inviting independent pilots to deliver bromellite, power generators, and thermal cooling units to Surveyor's Reach in Alrai in exchange for rewards including a class 5 pre-engineered cargo rack.
articles.player_impact: Independent pilots are invited to deliver construction commodities to Surveyor's Reach in Alrai. Contributors receive a class 5 pre-engineered cargo rack as reward. The expedition itself is scheduled to begin on January 18th.
articles.modern_impact: Establishes precedent for community-funded deep-space infrastructure. Future expeditions will likely replicate this crowdfunding model. The resulting station becomes a permanent frontier outpost supporting exploration in the galactic northeast.
articles.body_full:
The Distant Worlds working group has issued a call for mined and manufactured materials to support the construction of a new deep-space facility, intended to aid future exploration of remote galactic regions far beyond established survey routes.
Hermine Delarue, Executive Operative for Deep Space Surveys, stated:
“DSS has longstanding experience in supporting large-scale exploration efforts, most notably the construction of Explorers’ Anchorage during the Distant Worlds II initiative in 3305.”
“This new project focuses on preparing a remote site for long-range scientific operations. We aim to establish essential infrastructure for survey crews venturing into seldom-charted regions. Independent pilots are invited to help lay the foundations for the next era of deep-space discovery.”
Timotheus Haddard, quartermaster for an affiliated Distant Worlds support carrier, added:
“Initial requirements centre on core construction needs. We’re currently prioritising bromellite, power generators and thermal cooling units to begin establishing the primary framework.”
All interested parties have been invited to head to Alrai and register at Surveyor’s Reach before delivering the required commodities. DSS are reportedly offering a class 5 pre-engineered cargo rack to project contributors.
The expedition itself begins on the 18th of January, and organisers have issued an open invitation to any Commanders that wish to join the adventure.

articles.title: Distant Worlds Expedition Preparations Conclude Successfully
articles.summary: The Distant Worlds construction material appeal concludes successfully, with target quotas for power generators, bertrandite, and thermal cooling units met ahead of schedule. Hermine Delarue confirms the site has been surveyed and deep-range survey systems will be calibrated. Timotheus Haddard praises the coordinated response from haulers and escort wings. Contributing pilots may collect rewards at Surveyor's Reach in Alrai. The Distant Worlds III expedition is set to depart from NGC 1981 Sector ZU-Y d27 on January 18th.
articles.player_impact: Contributing pilots can collect rewards at Surveyor's Reach in Alrai. The expedition departs from NGC 1981 Sector ZU-Y d27 on January 18th, and all Commanders are invited to join.
articles.modern_impact: Demonstrates the logistical power of coordinated independent pilot networks. The DSS carrier logistics model may be replicated for future mega-expeditions, setting a new standard for civilian deep-space operations.
articles.body_full:
The Distant Worlds appeal for construction materials has concluded, with the initial infrastructure requested now fully delivered.
Organisers confirmed that target quotas for power generators, bertrandite and thermal cooling units were met ahead of schedule, with surplus supplies allocated for follow-on works.
Hermine Delarue, Executive Operative of Deep Space Surveys, issued the following statement:
“Commanders have once again demonstrated that the exploration community can build as well as discover. The core requisition targets are complete, the site has been fully surveyed, and our teams can now begin calibrating deep-range survey systems.”
“These foundations will support exploration efforts well beyond established scouting routes, with Deep Space Surveys continuing its work at the frontier.”
Timotheus Haddard, quartermaster for the Distant Worlds support carrier, also commented on the outcome:
“The logistical demands were significant and timelines were tight, but the response from independent pilots exceeded expectations. Material convoys arrived on schedule, and coordination between haulers and escort wings ensured steady delivery throughout the campaign.”
Contributing pilots can now collect their rewards at Surveyor’s Reach in Alrai.
A technical briefing on the completed works will be released once the new station has been deployed, which due to its deep space location, is estimated for March 3312.
Meanwhile, the Distant Worlds III expedition is set to begin tomorrow, departing  from the NGC 1981 Sector ZU-Y d27 system. All Commanders wishing to participate have been invited to join the expedition.
