articles.title: Laments in Witch-Space
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: On launch day of DW3 from NGC 1981 Sector ZU-Y d27, Jasmina Halsey aboard the Halsey's Quest experiences a profound witch-space anomaly during the fleet's mass jump. Multiple pilots report ghost echoes, voices on static, and ADC cross-talk. The cadence matches the Mars and Tionisla recordings—fifteen cycles exact. Hermine Delarue orders science framing as "Survey Refinement Alpha" while Halsey senses the presence feels grief and perplexity. The expedition adjusts its route toward the Umbra Sagittarii.
articles.player_impact: DW3 pilots were directed to tag and dump harmonic distortion recordings, attach raw wake scanner data, and log any anomalous experiences without chasing ghosts—contributing to a fleet-wide scientific survey of witch-space anomalies.
articles.modern_impact: This chapter documents the first confirmed fleet-wide witch-space anomaly during a mass jump, establishing that the phenomenon is not isolated to Halsey but affects multiple ships and pilots simultaneously, with a directional bias toward the galactic core.
articles.body_full:
NGC 1981 Sector ZU-Y d27, 3312 AD

The countdown rolled across every canopy like surf. On the main viewport the staging moon hung knife-bright, the armada strung about it in patient arcs, stars pinprick sharp in the backdrop.

The Halsey’s Quest’s bridge smelled of new plastics and warm metal, that particular mix ships have before they earn their grime. The Caspian was lean and purposeful with a forward gallery of glass looking out into the void. Conduits under the deck thrummed as the frame shift capacitors topped out, the FSD charge coil ticking as it bled heat into the keel.

“Wing leads green,” the comms officer reported. “Nav locks set. Wide-band clear. Mass locks show nominal.”

“Mass jump in five,” Captain Yuen said, not raising her voice. The sound carried anyway. “On my mark.”

Jasmina Halsey stood beside the rail with a borrowed headset and a view that would have made her twenty-year-old self weep. No Azalea to nudge her ribs with caution, no Cuthrick to fold a warning into a joke. They were back in Sol, shepherding the politics, holding the gates. She was here, a single presence wrapped in a new ship’s bones. The Quirium Control Unit sat in a foam cradle at her feet, sealed, inert, heavy as a thought.

“Three,” Yuen said.
“Two.”
“Punch.”

Frameshift pulled the stars to silk.

Witch-space opened, the corridor a familiar absence, the gentle throb of translation settling into the bones. The FSD’s phase coils found cadence against the tunnel wall, superluminal shear resolving to that almost-comforting bass roll every pilot learns to trust. Then the beat slid out of true. The corridor breathed in the wrong place. The auto-filter darkened the canopy against a flare that was not light as the bubble’s boundary shivered on the scopes.

“Hyperspace conduit integrity holding,” called the flight engineer, already leaning over a panel of ugly numbers. “Translation factor stable at point nine nine six.”

Jasmina did not need the recorder to tell her when it arrived. The pressure that haunted Olympus Village returned thicker, colder. A wash of not-sound crowded the edges of hearing. Words without language pressed towards her like a tide.

Grief.

“Low-band tick on harmonic grid,” the engineer muttered. “Fifteen again. Guardian booster notching but it is riding past the filter.”

“Shadow echo on wake three,” someone else said. “No object tracked. High-wake signature only.”

Open chatter bled through from wings off their bow.

“Anyone else seeing a reflection.”
“Ghost on the scopes. Fading.”
“I just heard… a voice. Like hearing your own name in a crowd.”

“Confirm faint modulation on ADC feed,” another voice added, professional and rattled. “Ship voice comms picking up cross-talk from the wake scanner. That is not supposed to happen.”

The conduit bucked once, corrected, then stuttered. Jasmina saw the HUD holofac flicker. A notch opened between beats as if a tooth slipped on a cog too large to see. In the notch something looked through her, not at the Halsey’s Quest but past it, the way weather fronts pass across oceans. Saturated with feeling. Tangled around a question it could not form. The Quirium unit at her feet gave the faintest pulse against the case foam like a cat butting a hand.

Jasmina closed her eyes. It made no difference. The corridor was inside her now.

You are not alone, she thought. We hear you.

The presence recoiled, not from her but from a pressure beyond them both. For a moment she sensed the rim of a larger shape, inevitability rather than malice. The consciousness folded itself small, like a hand snatching away from a flame it did not understand.

“Translation flicker,” said engineering. “Microdrop in containment at one part in ten thousand. AFMU is standing by. No faults logged.”

Normal space snapped back. A hard white star flooded the bridge. The Quest’s crew moved with that unshowy urgency good crews have, clearing boards, calling numbers, letting the heat sinks work instead of panicking them.

“Telemetry recorded,” said the engineer. “Clean capture on the trace. Wake scanner got a slice. Conduit-wall shear showed a blip.”

“Fifteen cycles exact,” comms confirmed. “Same cadence as Mars and Tionisla. Cross-checked against three hulls in our wing. Correlated, but the onboard chronometer desynced during transit. Updating now.”

Captain Yuen turned her chair half towards Halsey. “Madam Envoy?”

“Close enough to touch,” Jasmina said, steady because she had rehearsed being steady. “Grief and perplexity. It does not understand what is happening. It retreated.”

Yuen nodded once, as if someone had told her the weather would be foul on landing. “Log it. Stand by for supercruise.”

Hermine Delarue came up a breath later on the command frequency, silk over steel. “Science to fleet. If your recorder picked up harmonic distortion, tag and dump to DW3 archives. If your wake scanners flagged a cross-band echo, attach the raw. Voices on static, annotate the exact stamp from your flight recorder. Ghosts on scope, do not chase.”

Quartermaster Timotheus Haddard followed, his grin audible. “Logistics to fleet. If it felt weird, welcome to the tour. Refit windows open on the carrier from twenty to forty. If your AFMU threw a sulk after the jump get in line. Filter your complaints through science so I can blame our sponsors later.”

Jasmina muted the net and thumbed a private log. The words came clean.

She saved it and met the captain’s eye. “Captain Yuen, I will need a room with a map and two planners who hate surprises less than they say they do. And get Major Howard on comms. I hear she was at the Guardian ruins and hopefully has her logs from their scanning.”

The captain’s mouth gave the smallest ghost of a smile. “You will have it. Follow me.”

---
They took a glass-walled brief room immediately behind the bridge where the air still smelled of adhesive and fresh wiring. A star map unspooled along one wall. Two route planners hovered over it with the fussy tenderness of surgeons, overlays for scoopable stars and neutron superchargers already up. Hermine was there by telepresence, shoulders square, hair pinned by intent alone. Flight Major Elaine Howard had joined them on a secure line from her Whisky Wasp and Captain Yuen stood aside, looking at Jasmina.

“Show me the cadence,” Hermine said without preamble.

Jasmina pushed the packet. The display drew a clean band, then a bruise where the notch sat, then the smear that had made Martian engineers swear. Hermine dropped three anonymised traces on top. Different hulls, different drives, same wound in the rhythm.

“Voices on three,” Hermine said. “Ghost wake on seven. Two cases of ADC cross-talk. No pursuit, thank you. Correlation strongest in your wing, Envoy.”

“Fifteen on the miss again,“ Howard’s voice joined in. “We’ve seen that at the ruins, too, on the pico-hertz scale Ram Tah gave us. I’m going to have nightmares about that number. Any Thargoid signatures.” She waited a beat. “Good. Let us keep it that way.”

Fifteen…

Yuen folded her arms. “Madam Envoy, this is the same trace?”

“When we left Sol I could not find direction in it,” Jasmina said, with a nod. “Today there is a bias. Spinwise and coreward warms it. When I face the far northeast it sharpens like a tooth.’

Through her telepresence Hermine raised an eyebrow. “Interesting. I was recently told that region was called the Umbra Sagittarii once, the Archer’s Shadow. Basically, there be dragons. Fuel, spares, morale… it is a long way out. We do not peel an armada into the dark because a ghost asks nicely.”

“Who said that? The shadow I mean?” Jasmina demanded.

“One of our donors, although one of the odder ones. But he certainly knows a lot about early era space travel.” 

Howard literally could be heard rubbing her jaws over the comm. “DW3 already arcs that way. But we sure as hell didn’t gather three superpowers and a city of volunteers to ignore anomalies on day one. If we divert, how deep are you asking?”

“Far,” Jasmina said. “Where the survey routes thin to rumours.”

The planner glanced at the captain, then back to the map. “DW3 already trends spinwise and a touch coreward on the planned route. We can extend the reach without breaking the convoy. If we push a refinement branch we keep the route intact.”

“Options,” demanded the captain.

The senior planner traced a pale line with a fingertip. “We keep with the planned waypoints for now. From there we add a refinement: extra survey points step the convoy rimward and then back across. Fuel margins stay green based on K-class and scoopables on the leg. We can stitch in two neutron boosts to keep morale sweet and tanks fat.”

“Good,” Yuen said, then to Jasmina. “What do you think?”

“Yes,’ she said after a moment. ‘Feels right. The first step is almost on top of it. The second tells us if it sharpens or fades. The third is either the start of a map or proof we should not push. I should be able to triangulate as we proceed.”

“Science framing,” Hermine said. “We publish a dry note: anomalous witch-space signature detected, refinement added to collect comparative telemetry. No speculation. If you heard voices we need time stamps and raw. If you saw ghosts log, do not chase. If anyone writes the word ‘angel’ I will make them include a methods section and a double-blind.”

The captain looked to her comms officer. “Draft the fleet bulletin. Tag it Survey Refinement Alpha. Route planners lock the waypoints and push updates to every nav. Delarue you own the science packet. Howard you own the logs and cache timings. Everything goes through you. Madam Envoy…”

“I will ride the first leg and shut up unless the cadence moves,” Jasmina said.

“Good,” Yuen said, with a grin. “I like quiet envoys.”

The senior planner hesitated. “One more thing. If the anomaly links to jump distance we should vary the jump length a bit. Mix short and long transitions across the wing to see what resonates. We can also rotate Guardian FSD boosters in and out to see if the hybrid hardware changes the detection. Lots of variables to check.”

Hermine pointed. “Yes. Publish a pattern. Every third ship stretches one segment, every sixth compresses. Cross-index cadence against corridor length and Guardian hardware fit. Keep the variations small. I do not want cleverness.”

“Caspian hulls can take the long segment without sweating,” Howard said matter-of-factly. “I will tag three independents for the short hops. I have two pilots who fly like metronomes and one who thinks he is one. Probably Jacky Hew…”

“Add wake scanners to the lead elements,” the captain said. “If the corridor is bleeding into the scanner band I want it caught at source. Fit attenuation filters where you have them. No interdictions. We are not advertising a fight.”

“Mirrors to Alliance and Imperial science teams,” Hermine added. “Delayed, scrubbed, clean. No one cries foul later.”

“Do it,” the captain said.

---
The fleet bulletin dropped ten minutes later. A gentle chime rolled along the bridge. The comms officer read it once, then again, then nodded. “Survey Refinement Alpha published to all wings. Neutron boost brief added.”

Jasmina sent her field log to the DW3 buffer, a copy to Sol, one to Tionisla. Azalea’s reply arrived almost at once. Route accepted. Eat something. Sleep between legs. Cuthrick’s came a moment later. Your committees approve. I am bored already. Do something interesting and safe.

She smiled despite herself.

“Next mass jump in four,” Captain Yuen called, settling into her chair. “All wings report green. FSD charge at ninety-eight. Guardian boosters synced. Heatsinks cycled.”

The Halsey’s Quest’s bridge hushed in that way ships do when they listen to their own heartbeat. Outside, the armada slid into alignment, thousands of nav locks painting faint geometry across the dark.

Jasmina touched the rail, felt the paint still new under her fingers. The tug in her ribs was a thread now, not a pull, stretched toward the Archer’s Shadow. It did not feel like a destination. It felt like a question that had learned to wait.

“Wing leads green,” the comms officer said.
“Nav locks set. Wide-band clear.”
“Mass jump in five,” Yuen confirmed, the same even tone, the same weight. “On my mark.”

Jasmina steadied her breath. She had nothing to pray to so she counted, not the seconds but the beats of the drive, ready to catch the miss when it came.

“Three,” Yuen counted.
“Two.”
“Punch.”

Frameshift pulled the stars to silk. The corridor opened, the wake scanners sang in their leashes and the fleet leaned together into the dark.

Witch-space! We are coming!

articles.title: Le Quattro Stagioni
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: Hidden among the derelict ships of the Tionisla Orbital Graveyard, a mysterious young pilot in an outdated grey and green uniform listens to Vivaldi's Four Seasons by candlelight aboard his camouflaged vessel. When his console receives a coded Latin message—"Atra rota. Mundi distantes in motu sunt. Proceedite."—he responds in Italian, blows out the candles, and departs stealthily into witch-space.
articles.player_impact: The hidden operative's presence and coded communications suggest that shadowy organizations are tracking or manipulating the DW3 expedition from concealed positions within the Graveyard.
articles.modern_impact: This interlude introduces an unidentified operative with anachronistic technology and cryptic communications, hinting at deeper layers of surveillance and manipulation surrounding the expedition that operate outside known power structures.
articles.body_full:
Tionisla, after Launch Day

The scenery outside was melancholic; the system’s orange sun was far away and it barely illuminated all the bizarre metal carcasses. The place was full of them, as far as the eye — or the ship canopy’s enhanced visual sensors — could see; hundreds if not thousands of ancient space hulks and star fighters, floating at one of the Lagrange points in the star system’s complicated orbits. Derelict ships of all models and ages slowly rotated in a perennial danse macabre, disturbed only occasionally by the local security patrols that struggled to deter scavengers, adventurous tourists and, more recently, Federation officials and their patchwork entourage. 

One of the ships deep inside this belt of metal corpses danced the same dance, but it was intact and occupied. It rolled with a gentle five percent pitch, perfectly mimicking its defunct companions. Every once in a while the shadows of its bigger neighbours fell over the hull, covering it in utter darkness. A few minutes later they would retreat again to let the dim sunlight reflect off the ship’s hull once more. 

Inside, most of its systems had been deactivated, including the cockpit lights. Observers would likely have smiled at the pair of wax candles on a candelabra resting on the dashboard. The flickering lights danced across the cockpit’s consoles and, along with the ship’s gentle roll, they seemed to hold its pilot in a trance. He sat in the pilot’s chair, apparently oblivious to his surroundings.

Soft music filled the cockpit with the delicate and ancient sound of string instruments: Le Quattro Stagioni, the four seasons, an impossibly old piece of art composed by a long-dead genius, who would never have imagined his concerti would be listened to inside a lone spaceship more than 1,500 years later.  

The pilot was young for a Commander, although his outfit suggested otherwise: he wore some sort of outdated dark grey and green uniform with fingerless gloves. His flight suit may have been fashionable in the eighties. He was not tall, and had short, curly, black hair. A moustache and a chin beard completed the sly, roguish appearance. 

An observer may have guessed he was meditating to the intense music. He absently held a glass of red wine in his right hand, resting his chin in his left. The glass had a lid and a straw. Every once in a while he turned the glass a few degrees and looked at the wine drops bouncing inside. The music and tranquil setting seemed to consume him wholly.

Suddenly, one of the console lights flashed red, and an audio-mechanic beep disrupted the melodious ambience. 

“Ah, no! No, no, no!”

Annoyed, the pilot exploded from his meditation, nearly letting the glass go. With a hissed curse he shook his head, reached forward and switched one of the small mechanical levers on the console.

Abruptly, the music ceased. He sat upright and pulled his flight seat closer to the console. A ‘click’ somewhere signalled the re-routing of the ship’s comm system and next, a single, distorted voice echoed from the speakers:

“Atra rota. Mundi distantes in motu sunt. Procedite.”

Still annoyed, the pilot put down his glass of red wine, reached over to the console again and switched the lever in the opposite direction.

“Okay, okay. Digli che sto arrivando.”

The pilot put his glass in one of the cup-holders to his right and blew out the candles. He pulled one of the overhead levers and the ship stopped to roll. When he was sure the rotation had come to a halt he cautiously moved the power controller forward until the navigation panel came online. A number of blips appeared in a holographic sphere above the panel. He took a few moments to study their movements; they were security patrols on duty, their trajectories routine. 

“Merda.”

He activated the bow thrusters. There was the sound of machinery in the bowels of his venerable ship, as it began to move backwards. When it was clear of a neighbouring Boa freighter, the pilot relaxed. The huge ship would provide him with a decent sensor shadow to all but the keenest observers. Finally, he powered the hyperdrive and began his calculations for a jump trajectory. 

A few minutes later he was gone and the ship cemetery was left to itself again.

articles.title: “Ventura Transformation” Video Goes Viral
articles.summary: Actor William 'Big Bill' Ventura's self-produced workout video goes viral, showing dramatic body transformation. Millions of followers adopting regimen. Plans to hike Lave rainforests for conservation.
articles.player_impact: Cultural event. Viral fitness trend from actor William Ventura. Millions of responses. No direct gameplay but may tie to future Radicoida or commodity storylines.
articles.modern_impact: Celebrity-driven wellness phenomenon foreshadows potential commodification of performance enhancement. The trend's unusual consistency across professions and Dr. Casimir's later dismissal as 'diet meds and confidence tricks' suggests an underlying tension between organic and pharmaceutical enhancement narratives that may resurface.
articles.body_full:
A health-conscious video recorded by holovid action star William “Big Bill” Ventura has gone viral on interstellar networks, sparking a wave of positivity.
Known for comedic roles in traditional ‘real cast’ productions such as ‘Malacticus Runs Again’ and ‘For A Few Credits Less’, Ventura’s notoriously vibrant party lifestyle has often made him a popular figure of fun and mischief in many celebrity gossip sections.
But a recent self-produced video of Ventura’s workout regimen has exploded in popularity, with the actor showing a remarkable body transformation to lean, fit and strong.
“I’ve dedicated the past year to improving myself after growing unhappy with my image,” Ventura told Corinne Macintyre of the Alliance Tribune. “My energy levels have been through the roof, and after putting in so much effort I feel like I can achieve anything! I want to hike across the rainforests of Planet Lave in support of ongoing conservation efforts there.”
Messages of support and clips of people following Ventura’s workouts have poured in, with millions of responses attributed to the original video. Ventura called the response ‘mind-blowing, just crazy to see so much love and healthy choices resulting from all this.’

articles.title: At Jaques
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: The DW3 convoy arrives at Colonia. Jacky Hew entertains pilots with stories while Halsey meets Jaques, who reports strange equipment behavior—docking computers "growing feelings," nav-buoys claiming to be cargo racks, and a Scottish-singing voice alarm. The anomalies intensified after a Pilots' Federation Eridanus-class exploration cruiser uploaded survey data. Jaques introduces Halsey to Alessia Verdi, an Imperial pilot who witnessed Salomé's death and agrees to help Halsey navigate Imperial political currents. A wake scanner picks up the fifteen-cycle echo near Colonia.
articles.player_impact: Pilots in the Colonia region reported anomalous equipment behavior and cross-band echoes, contributing data that helped trace the witch-space anomaly's spread along the expedition route.
articles.modern_impact: The chapter reveals that the witch-space anomaly is not confined to jump corridors but affects station equipment and hardware near locations where large survey datasets were processed—suggesting a data-transmissible or EM-responsive component.
articles.body_full:
Colonia, 3312 AD

The big ships slid in on tidy vectors, heat blooms restrained, wakes braided so as not to rattle the locals. After the first week the corridor had stopped bucking. The fifteen-cycle miss still showed up now and then, a smudge in the low band, but it had become background hiss. Pilots stopped murmuring about ghosts and went back to arguing about jumponium routes, the latest SRV racing results and who had the better synth-coffee machines on their Kraits.

By the time the convoy crossed the last stretch to the Colonia Bridge, bar talk had cooled. A notorious carouser named Jacky Hew decided to fix that. Jacky held court on all of the four Distant Worlds carriers, making the rounds and gathering in the drinks.

“Carrier jumps are different, kids,” he announced to the room, pint aloft. “You pack your whole bad decision into a moving rock and fling it at the sky. No romance. Now, back in the day when I scouted the Neutron Highway—”

Groans rose like a litany from the assembled crowds, but they were up for a bit of entertainment after being cooped up in their cockpits for days on end. Jasmina sat at the back, inconspicuous, and happy to be part of the scenery. But she watched everything going on around her. People watching, particularly spacers and pilots, could reveal things…

“—you learned the smell of your FSD cooking itself to jerky. You snorted cone plots like spice. You rode the superflares till your eyebrows went wobbly. If the ship didn’t try to kill you twice before breakfast you were still docked.”

Someone shouted that Jacky had been docked more often than not. Jacky bowed to the accusation and drank to it.

“Point is,” he said, leaning in as if sharing state secrets, “I’ve seen drives sing when they shouldn’t, and I’ve seen them sulk when paid. But I’ve also heard weird whispers out here. Kit going wonky across a few Colonia stations. Docking computers that fancy themselves poets. Cartographic terminals freezing like they remembered something they shouldn’t.”

That last line found more ears than it should have. Jasmina leant forward a touch.

“Maybe someone ought to have a look around,” Jacky added, casual and sharp at once. “That’s all I’m saying…”

---
---
Jaques Station filled the canopy like a huge misshapen scar of a station, skin stippled with repair plates, lights running along its flanks like the memory of tides. Halsey took the call from a quiet corner of the Caspian ship’s bridge rather than her cabin. It felt right to keep the stars in view while speaking to a man who had once flown himself across half the galaxy.

The holo resolved to a face part flesh part alloy. Servo-lines traced from a chrome cheek-plate to the temple where a pale optical implant irised against the link’s light. A sub-vocal modulator gave his words a second undertone like valves warming.

“Madam Envoy,” Jaques said, amused rather than formal. The metal in his jaw clicked once as he smiled. “Welcome back to the colony that isn’t a colony.”

“Just a waypoint that learned to have opinions,” Halsey said. “Good to see you, Jaques.”

“Likewise. I hear you brought an entire entourage with you. Try not to jam all the pads?’

“We will be polite,” she promised. “I need your help. We have been chasing a cadence. I hear there’s been the odd strange thing noted at your end of the map.”

Jaques cocked his head. Tiny servos whirred as the optical implant refocused. “You heard about the gear behaving like it grew feelings?”

“Jacky Hew was flapping his mouth,” she said.

“Yes, he does that,” Jaques replied, the modulator colouring the consonants. “He is not wrong about this though. We have had intermittent misbehaviour. Nothing that breaks a ship. Everything that irritates an engineer. Docking towers that refuse a pad allocation until you swear at them. Power relays that forget their friends. The odd nav-buoy claiming it is a cargo rack. My favourite is a voice alarm that went from traffic advisory to singing a line from some ancient Scottish melody. No obvious pattern, but there is a shape to the places.”

“Which places?”

“Started as whispers at outposts along the lane,” Jaques said. He glanced off-screen and a retinal HUD flickered in the implant’s lens. “Then we started hearing it in the station. And the timing, Jasmina. Odd. No spikes during your approach. But when the Pilots’ Federation exploration cruiser came through. Big. Proud. Eridanus class. Bristling with long-range survey kit. They did the round of the local systems. Next morning they uploaded a mountain of data to Universal Cartographics. Top tier. Straight to my station. Cost me a fortune. After that the gremlins woke up.”

“You’re sure about the timing?”

“All bartenders have good clocks,” he said. The metal jaw clicked again, a habit more than a fault. “They walked the data to UC in the afternoon. That night I started getting reports of nonsense. Day after that two ships reported their surface scanners were hearing background music on surface scans. Just weird behaviour…”

“Any common fit in the pattern of weirdness?”

“Mostly modern drives,” Jaques said. “Half the ships here have bolted Guardian wake tat to their hulls in the last few years so we see a lot of hybrids. I cannot prove correlation. I can tell you two PF officers were in the bar talking about a Guardian Beacon out in the dark. Said it was ‘strange’ when they pinged it on their way in. One of them mentioned a DSSA carrier further north on the map. They want to liaise before they go and spend two years making friends with K-type stars.”

“Strange...” Jasmina said. “Like you say, lots of pieces, no pattern. Can we help? What do you need?”

“What I need is for everything to behave,” Jaques said with a dry little harmonics-wobble from the modulator. “Failing that, get your massive bunch of scientists to scan my house and garden. Keep it honest. Run a wake net round the station. Sniff my nav-buoys. Sample the EM in the docking approach.”

“Perimeter or close?”

“Both. Hell, scan everything in Colonia if you have the time. We need to know if this is local mischief or if the smear has a radius,” he said. The eye-implant shuttered and opened. “I can give you priority station time.”

“I’ll see what we can do.”

“And if your numbers match the gossip you will want to know what those PF officers saw when they went poking at Guardian hardware.”

“I will want to know that anyway. Do you have their names?” Jasmina asked.

“The cruiser left but I still have their call signs on a cocktail bill. I will forward them. And a suggestion.” A faint servo-hum underscored the pause. “If you hear echoes from the the void do not stand still too long. Whatever is making our wires itch did not start here.”

“Agreed.”

“Good. Dock your expedition,” Jaques said. The alloy cheek caught the holo’s glow as he dipped his head. “And Jasmina… if the ghosts want to sing, please make them keep to key. By the way, you should visit my bar. There’s someone here I think you should meet.”

Jasmina was about to ask who, but the holofac communication had already flickered off.

---
The bar sat in the crook of a support rib where the station’s bones showed through the cladding. Lamps made from old nav beacons threw warm cones of light. The room smelled of coolant, burnt coffee and citrus cleaner that tried its best. A low thread of conversation ran under a shipboard blues track that never quite resolved.

Jaques eased through the crowd with the easy authority of a man who had poured a million drinks. Jasmina followed him through the jostling mass of people. The alloy in Jaques’ jaw clicked once as he smiled.

“Jasmina,” he said, pitching his voice for her ear alone. “Over here. Her name is Alessia Verdi. Imperial. Flies like she has somewhere to be and a grudge for company. She’s been here a few times before. Knows her ships. Has stories… if she’s here in Colonia, it means something. She only just made the last fleet carrier out of the bubble – last minute decision to tag along? Might be related, might not. Worth checking.”

Jasmina looked where Jaques gestured.

The woman at the bar rail had the lean look of long patrols and stress. Flight leathers scuffed white at the seams. A silver signet at her throat. She watched the room as if the room might try something. When she turned her head Halsey saw the small Imperial crest tattooed just inside the hairline. Old ink. Earned, not bought. Grey hair and grey eyes marked a face that had been young not that long ago, but had been aged prematurely by grief and strife.

Jaques introduced them, providing both with a drink.

“Madam Envoy,” Alessia said. The vowels were clipped Achenar. “Or do you prefer Jasmina like the GalNet liars?”

“Jasmina will do,” Halsey said. “Jaques tells me you barely made the last ride out of the bubble.”

A shrug. “I’m fashionably late. I do not like crowds. The fleet is a crowd with engines. Colonia was quieter before. This expedition changed that.”

“You came anyway.”

“I have my reasons.” Alessia said. “It’s clearer out here in the void. Jaques’ whisky is bad, but the coffee is ok.”

Jaques let that sit. Alessia gave him a suggestive look. The servos behind his eye implant ticked as he checked a ghost HUD only he could see. “I will refresh my reputation with the bar,” he said mildly, and drifted away.

Alessia watched him go then put her elbows on the rail. “He is smarter than he looks,” she said. “And a lot older than most realise.”

Halsey took the spot beside her. The window behind the bar showed a sliver of the docking axis. A Type-9 drifted through the slot like a stubborn planet.

“Jaques said you had history,” Halsey said. “That you’re someone I should know.”

“History is the polite word,” Alessia said. Her mouth did not soften. “You have heard the latest rumours. The dead walk. Titles crawl out of graves. Salomé returns to judge the living.”

“Kahina Tijani Loren,” Halsey said. “The enigmatic Salomé. I remember the broadcasts. But that was years ago. She was shot down… some say she committed suicide, others that she faked her death and is still alive…”

Alessia’s knuckles whitened on the rail. The tendons in her hands drew tight, then let go. “I was there,” she said. “I saw her die. Not a myth. Not a holo. Blood and vacuum. She’s gone.”

Jasmina could see the haunted look in the other woman’s eyes.

“You followed her.”

“She was my friend.”

Jasmina could see Alessia’s jaws clench. She looked away before speaking again.

“I believed she would make an Empire worth fighting for,” Alessia said. “Expose the wrongs… and right them. I was wrong about that – wrong about a lot of things. Salomé failed. She let us down, all of us. Then others made a business out of her death. She was not the paragon of virtue she has been idolised as. I was caught up in the worship like so many others, I was young, stupid and naive. I made mistakes. I’ve paid for them ever since. I don’t follow saviours anymore.”

The bitterness was clean. Not theatrical. A slow acid that had eaten its way to daylight.

“Then why chase a convoy into deep space,” Halsey asked. “Why are you here? Because of Salomé?”

“Because I know what it looks like when a story gets written over the top of the truth,” Alessia said. “Your fleet is going somewhere important. Half the officers in every club from Cubeo to Sothis are already writing the ending for you. I would rather see what is really happening. I don’t know what you are chasing, probably I don’t need to, but this is not just an exploration trip and it feels like it did back then… secrets in the darkness waiting to be found. Danger lurking, people scheming… I had to come.”

They let the music hold the next moment. The singer found a line about lost systems and debts unpaid. Halsey watched Alessia’s face find and lose a dozen replies.

“You know the Empire,” Halsey said. “Imperial currents. Who listens. Who pretends not to. If I needed to put a word in a specific ear without leaving fingerprints could you help me?”

Alessia did not look surprised. “You mean could you use me as a lever?”

“I was trying to be subtle.”

“I have a highly tuned bullshit detector,” Alessia snapped. “I knew the moment Jaques offered me a free drink. Everyone wants something, you’re no different.”

“If it keeps pilots alive,” Halsey said. “If it keeps the science honest...”

A long look. Not hostile. Measuring weight and cost.

“I am not a diplomat,” Alessia said at last. “I am good at making a message feel like gossip and letting it land where it should. I can tell you who is compromised and who isn’t. I can do that. But I will not lie for you – you’re not worth it, no one is.”

“I will not ask you to,” Halsey said.

“Good,” Alessia said. “Then here is some free advice. Those who trade in legends are already tacking Salomé’s name to your story. They will say the Caretakers spoke to her first, or some other spacer crap. They will say she’s somehow wrapped up in all this, that she’s running the expedition in secret – they love their conspiracy theories! They still treat her like a fallen goddess whose name will never die. You will not win by arguing with that. You will only win by using that to your advantage.”

Halsey felt a small involuntary smile. “Hermine will approve of your method.”

“Who?”

“Hermine Delarue, our operations lead,” Halsey said. “She hates anything she can’t stick a gauge on.”

“Then she and I will get along if we never meet,” Alessia said. The corners of her mouth twitched. It did not get as far as a smile.

Jaques returned with two short glasses and a nod to the tender. Steam rose from one. The other held something that looked like it had been aged inside a thruster bell.

“House policy,” he said. “First drink after a long road is on me if you promise not to break my station. You will like the coffee. Alessia will pretend not to like the whisky.”

Alessia took the glass and did not pretend. “Salud,” she said. “No legends, just people.”

“No legends,” Halsey echoed.

They drank. The whisky carried a quiet burn that did not argue. The coffee was bitter in a way that felt useful.

Alessia set her glass down and faced Halsey without the rail between them. “If you find a truth out there,” she said, “let me know and say it plain. We can work with plain, we choke on riddles.”

“I will say it plain,” Halsey said. “And if I need a word whispered?”

“I’m on the expedition,” Alessia replied. “I’ll be at the back most likely. Keeping an eye on things. You’ll be able to find me.”

Jasmina nodded.

“Oh, and one more thing,” Alessia said.

Jasmina looked back at her.

“Do not underestimate the power of myth,” Alessia said. “Salomé is dead, but in all the years since that hasn’t slowed her down one bit…”

---
Halsey kept her own role small. She visited the tower to drink station air and thank the crews for accommodating the mass of DW3 ships flooding the docks. She walked the concourse and watched the flow around the terminals without stepping too close. She stood on a viewing deck where the window glass had been etched by a thousand small collisions and looked down at the moving geometry of approach lights and landing gear.

When the first returns came in they were boring, which is what you want your first returns to be. A clean wake net. EM sweeps with a few hairs in the comb where the spines hummed against their brackets. Buoy traffic within noise tolerances, save for a packet with a timing smear that a junior tech flagged as “ugly but harmless.”

Then a pilot called Alistair Brodey, flying an Eagle with an engineered wake scanner, pinged a comm.

“Operations, you want this,” Brodey said, half-whispered awe threading through professionalism. “Wake scanner just picked up… something. Cross-band echo at fifteen cycles. Same miss. It is faint but it is there.”

Hermine’s reply was a heartbeat quick, silk turned to wire. “Brodey? Didn’t know you were out there. Tag, stamp, push raw. Repeat sweep. Anyone else with a wake focus near that local, get me more data.”

Two more ships caught it on the next pass. Not loud. Not dramatic. A fingertip on a drum. Fifteen.

Halsey stood very still in the crowd and imagined a lattice pulled like a net over a town, small ripples turning cutlery in drawers, lights that forget their names for a second then remember. She imagined a cruiser bristling with instruments walking a mountain of maps into a hungry machine and the hungry machine humming back in a key no one could hear until now.

Her console chimed. A text from Jaques. Thought so… whatever this is, it’s not from here, but it’s been here…

Halsey exhaled, steady. “Captain Yuen,” she said into the ship line, “let’s see where the nice PF cruiser went sightseeing. Jaques said ‘north’ and DSSA is involved so give them a call. And send the wake scans home to Lya, see what she can figure out. She still has all the Guardian data from that Engineer. See if it sings out of tune.”

The tug at her ribs had not strengthened, but it had learned to tap once in every so many beats. Colonia was a pause and a welcome rest, not an answer.

“On your mark,” the captain said.

“Engage,” Halsey replied, and the DW3 machine prepared to face the next question.

articles.title: Genetic Study of Radicoida Unica Released
articles.summary: Dr. Roy Casimir publishes first public Radicoida unica study. Mercurial genetic composition, symbiotic potential with creatures, and performance-enhancing seed pod compounds discovered. Lexi October claims competent oversight.
articles.player_impact: First public study of Radicoida unica released. Plant shows symbiotic potential and seed pods contain performance-enhancing compounds. Data partially redacted by October Consortium. No human trials imminent.
articles.modern_impact: First public data on Radicoida unica seeds a future pharmacological research arms race. October Consortium's data redaction hints at proprietary military or civilian enhancement applications. The seed pod compounds' ability to improve physical performance and reduce thinking time could eventually see widespread use or restriction.
articles.body_full:
The first publicly available study of Radicoida unica has been published following heavy pressure from the exobiological community.
Radicoida unica, a huge plant unique to the HIP 87621 system, has attracted intense speculation over its properties and applications. It has been deemed worthy of prolonged military action by major powers seeking to establish control of territory around the system.
Dr. Roy Casimir, chief researcher at the Holloway Bioscience Institute, has released a study of Radicoida unica based on data provided by October Consortium, which currently claims legal ownership of HIP 87621.
“Our findings indicate a remarkable genetic composition which I can only describe as mercurial. The cellular resilience and adaptability of Radicoida unica is breathtaking, even when compared to other notable stellar phenomena we have catalogued thus far.”
“October Consortium researchers highlight observations that the plant may form symbiotic relationships with biological creatures with prolonged exposure. It seems aware of activity around it, and has a flowering season where seed pods are produced. The flesh of these pods is what truly excites me – it contains a compound which improves physical performance and reduces thinking time in laboratory mice, for example. A plethora of possible medical uses has been attached, and some proposed ideas are fascinating.”
Dr. Casimir noted that the data provided to the Holloway Institute was curated by October Consortium, and some aspects were redacted. This was attributed to standard proprietary data protection.
Lexi October made a statement to coincide with Dr. Casimir’s, claiming that this data sharing was further evidence of October Consortium’s competent oversight of HIP 87621.

articles.title: Coalition Announces Non-Aggression Pact Amid HIP 87621 Hostilities
articles.summary: Coalition of major powers announces non-aggression pact in HIP 87621 enclave. Aisling, Grom, Arissa, Kaine, Mahon and Patreus aligned. Antal excluded. Analysts suggest motive is to refocus on core system conflicts.
articles.player_impact: Non-aggression pact in HIP 87621 enclave between Aisling Duval, Yuri Grom, Arissa Lavigny-Duval, Nakato Kaine, Edmund Mahon and Denton Patreus forces. Pranav Antal excluded. Fighting subsides but sporadic clashes continue.
articles.modern_impact: Informal power coalition without Federal representation shifts the post-war superpower balance. Exclusion of Pranav Antal and the Federation creates new diplomatic fault lines. This model of independent pilot-led peace agreements may influence how future enclave conflicts are resolved without direct superpower intervention.
articles.body_full:
The group, comprising of Aisling Duval, Yuri Grom, Arissa Lavigny-Duval, Nakato Kaine, Edmund Mahon and Denton Patreus aligned forces, brings together representatives and affiliated factions to agree to an informal non-aggression pact. The agreement is described as intending to guarantee mutual support and reduce further escalation in the enclave. Pranav Antal's forces were notably missing from the announcement, with rumours circulating that Antal has not been included in the Pact following the two-week ceasefire.
Speaking to Vox Galactica, a spokesperson for the coalition claimed that it represents an independently organised group of pilots, arguing that coordinated restraint is necessary to try to avoid any further confrontation in the enclave.
However, political analysts have been quick to temper such claims.
Current assessments indicate that the majority of systems surrounding HIP 87621 remain under Imperial control, with Nakato Kaine, Yuri Grom and Pranav Antal retaining influence in limited sections of the enclave.
The pact applies to pledged forces and independent pilots specifically within the enclave area. Analysists suggest that an ulterior motive for the pact is to allow renewed focus on conflicts within the core systems.
War correspondent Ernesto Rios commented:
“The non-aggression pact introduces an unexpected variable as large-scale engagements in the enclave appear to be winding down. It remains unclear how this arrangement affects October Consortium’s authority within HIP 87621, or how long these coalition pilots will maintain their discipline.”
“Questions also remain regarding the Imperial government response, particularly given that the agreement was reached independently without direct instruction from the Emperor when strategic dominance appeared within reach.”
Although fighting has largely subsided, sporadic clashes continue in outlying systems. With growing scrutiny over Radicoida unica’s recently reported properties, observers caution that the current lull may prove temporary, and the threat of wider conflict remains.

articles.title: Rumors in the Black
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: The DW3 flotilla searches for the missing Universal Cartographics cruiser Guinevere at a Rendezvous Point. Lya advises searching K-type stars for beacon pings. CMDR Nor discovers a damaged DSSA beacon with a dead man's voice recording. Lya's analysis back-traces the beacon's trajectory to permit-locked systems in the Praei2 sector. Hermine reveals Cal warned her about the Umbra Sagittarii. The expedition prepares to investigate while maintaining public survey operations.
articles.player_impact: DW3 pilots conducted wide cone sweeps and passive wake scans to locate the missing cruiser, with CMDR Nor finding the critical beacon that redirected the search toward permit-locked space.
articles.modern_impact: The chapter reveals that a Universal Cartographics deep space cruiser disappeared near a permit-locked sector, and that someone—possibly DSSA itself—deployed a crudely built emergency beacon while concealing the incident from official records.
articles.body_full:
Rendezvous Point, 3313 AD, Supercruise

The flotilla slid into formation like a school of bright fish. Wake geometry braided thin so as not to rattle the stragglers. Ahead, the primary star burned a comfortable white, its chart label on every canopy simply reading the bookmarked location: Rendezvous Point.

“Area sweep as per plan,” Captain Yuen said. “Wide cone, wake net at twenty-kilometre intervals. Keep your scanners sharp. The search is underway.”

Halsey watched the traffic bloom on the tactical. Caspian hulls peeled off in pairs, independents filled the gaps. She felt the tug in her ribs soften to the background. Quieter here. Nothing like what she had sensed before.

She raised an eyebrow at that and then looked over to the captain. “How soon will we know?”

“Depends on whether there’s anything to find,” the captain murmured.

For many hours, nothing came back. No signs, no anomalies, no signal sources worthy more than a cursory examination. Jasmina helped herself to a coffee and then called up the holofac transmitters.

Timotheus Haddard, the Distant Sun’s quartermaster, came in on the logistics net, less grin than usual. “DSSA reps on our carriers have been helpful to a fault but none can find the callsign for this carrier. I am getting shrugs and polite bafflement. That is not a combination I enjoy.”

“I can help with that,” Hermine said. “My contacts back in the bubble have just told me our mystery ship is the Universal Cartographics cruiser, Guinevere. Eridanus-class. Two-year assignment filed with the Pilots’ Federation Logistics Board. Survey scope: K-type primaries, high probability of undiscovered terraformables and pristine rings.”

“Sounds right,” Jasmina said, with a nod. “That tallies with what I know. Does it help us find it?”

“Not really,” Timotheus replied. “But it will help narrow things down if we do encounter a wreck or a beacon.”

“Can we narrow the search area somehow?” Hermine asked.

Jasmina thought for a moment.

“How about our lead astrophysicist?” she asked. “Lya might have…”

Hermine rolled her eyes.

“Really? The lead astrophysicist who hates space?”

“I admit she’s unconventional,” Jasmina replied. “But space is big… we need to narrow our focus…”

“Theory never beats practical experience,” Hermine said. “It’s all very well sitting back home in the safety of your nice warm ivory tower while real explorers take the actual risks…”

“I think she can help us,” Jasmina said, softly.

Hermine shrugged. Jasmina keyed the holofac and another figure joined the telepresence.

The wall-sized holo on the bridge flickered to a woman in her early thirties with bright blonde hair in a disciplined bun and the expression of someone who really objected to any kind of face to face communication.

“Lya,” Jasmina said. “We’re hooked up with Timotheus and Hermine.”

“Awesome! The TelePros seem to be aligned just fine!” Lya said. “Lovely to see you too, Timetheus.” She paused. “Oh, and Hermine I see. All well?”

Hermine narrowed her eyes. Timotheus shifted from side to side.

“So far so good,” Jasmina said. “We’re hoping you can help us.”

Jasmina quickly brought her up to speed.

“Lya, your floor. Anything you’ve got would be helpful.”

“Splendid! And thanks for thinking of me from so far away!” Lya said. “Well, if the Guinevere was on a K-type survey mandate then she’ll have left fingerprints. K-primaries sit in a sweet spot for water worlds and ELWs. Cartographics cruisers do not just honk and go. They park. They probe. They leave away teams and drop scanner packages. That’s UniCart 101. They run multi-band probes on the rings and they drape a net of beacon pings across the whole place. There will be some evidence of where they are and where they went.”

She blinked at someone off camera and then nodded before turning back to the holofac. “I’d suggest doing something similar out there. You need to fly in your wing thingies and survey K-type stars within one jump of your current location. Or two… Or make it three. Run discovery scans but prioritise space signals and non-standard broadbands. Wake scanners in passive mode. If you have any Guardian wake enhancements, leave them bolted on to the FSS. K-types are EM noisy but they are honest. You’ll find a clue, I promise.”

Jasmina nodded. Timotheus looked optimistic. Hermine looked skeptical.

“We’ll try,” Jasmina said. ‘Thankyou.”

“Most welcome,” Lya said. “Oh, and relay me all their astro spreadsheets if you find any. Ivory tower, out.”

The holofac faded. Timotheus stifled a laugh.

Jasmina smiled and then gestured to the captain.

Captain Yuen nodded. “We’ll break the fleet into three sweeps. Leave it with me and Howard.”

---
They found the beacon on the second day after arrival.

Nor — a pilot from Colonia — was the first to catch it. “Science, I have a broadband squawk at 12.2 kHz above the soup. Wide and ugly. And odd. Modulation looks distressed. Origin near the ecliptic.”

“Mark and hold,” Hermine said. “Do not touch. Fleet, we have a live one. Passive only.”

Captain Yuen bled the engines down to a sensible speed. The K-type primary filled half the canopy, an amber patience. Off to port a freckle of manufactured light blinked, wrong in cadence and colour.

“Range ten,” the helm called. “Scoop deployed. No grav anomalies.”

“Nice and smooth. Putting it in the cargo bay,” comms said.

There was a faint clunk from somewhere below the bridge.

“Let’s go,” Jasmina said, heading towards the rear.

The beacon was nothing the team anticipated. It was more akin to a satellite, ancient and comparably crude. Its casing had been patched with what looked like duct tape and angry welding. This was neither an emergency beacon nor was it contemporary ship equipment in any way. The paint on the side had once been fashionably orange. Someone had stencilled a half visible and discomforting “DSSA” with an Arc Cutter on its metal belly. 

Jasmina’s stomach clenched. “This…,” she pointed at the satellite. “I have seen this before. I just…”

“Wideband,” the engineer interrupted when he got a chance to inspect it in the cargo bay. “No handshakes. No key. Badly damaged, but I think I can… yeah, here we go…”

The beacon suddenly spoke in bursts. A dead man’s voiceline, stitched and stretched.

The cargo bay went quiet in that way ships do when everyone is listening to the same ghost.

“Again,” Jasmina said, softer. “Can you augment the audio at all?”

They let it roll until the clock said it had repeated three times exactly, but it was no clearer. The captain lifted a hand. “Take a break. Science has the raw. I’ll make a note to thank CMDR Nor, that was a lucky find.”

“I’ll pull the casing,” the engineer said. “Might be able to salvage something more from it.”

Jasmina nodded absently.

The camera drone slid close and took the kind of images administrators love. Scoring on the data plate. A fleet maintenance sticker, six months old. The DSSA crest stamped off-center by someone having a bad day.

“Any locator?” Hermine asked.

“Nope,” the engineer said. “But the configuration is odd. I mean steel and titanium plating? Hello 34th century? A lot of damage here, understandably, but some of the data core is intact so at least the shielding held. But again, no proto or radiolytic alloys? Who built this thing? And more importantly, when? But we’ll probably need more compute power than we can summon out here in the void.”

“Extract what you can,” Jasmina said. “We’ll send it to Lya and see what she can make of it.”

Hermine sighed. “So she can save the day again from the comfort of her armchair.”

---
Back in the bubble Lya had wasted no time. Analysts in fleet jumpsuits and borrowed lab coats fed the beacon data into a dozen open mouths of software and let them chew.

“Spectral first,” Lya said. “The beacon’s wideband is trash but trash has fingerprints. Look for sidebands no one asked for. Look for a carrier…” She chuckled. “...on the carrier.”

Numbers stacked, data flowed, screens plotted graphs. An analyst raised a hand. “There is a comb at forty-two hertz riding the entire packet. Six teeth. Equal spacing. Could be chassis vibration, could be an intentional watermark.”

“Could be a wake bleed,” someone else said. “Fifteen shows up faint.”

“Note it, but do not fall in love with it,” Lya said. “Temporal next.”

They pinned the repeats in time and found a micro-drift where none should have been. The kind of drift you get when your clock comes from the sky and the sky has been bent.

“Plot this on the galactic chart,” Lya said. “If the beacon floated a while before it got tired and started yelling then solar wind should have pushed it. Solve for deployment point by back-tracing on the minor outgassing we can hear in the noise.”

Lines darted, then erased, then came back thicker. A ghost-trajectory painted itself across the holofac. It did not point back to the Rendezvous Point. It curled spinwise and up, toward a pane of the map that had always been a polite blank.

“Again,” Lya said. “Assume the deployment was deliberate. Weighted throw calculations. Give me a cone, not a line.”

The cone grew, faint and infuriating. At its thin end a cluster of systems lit up in pale triangles. All of them wore the same quiet label every pilot knows and then pretends not to be interested in.

Permit-locked.

“Well, well, well… Curiouser and curiouser,” Lya breathed.

---
Later that day Lya made her report.

Hermine drew a breath. “Names?”

The system designations scrolled past like a list you only see when you have done something to earn a look. Among them, a map name floated up from the archives like a fish coming to bread.

“Praei2,” Lya read. “Someone had a laconic week. It’s a permit-locked sector in the northern pane.”

Hermine looked alarmed for a moment. Jasmina felt the tug in her ribs tap once, as if in approval.

Yes, this is it…

Flight Major Elaine Howard broke the silence before it got ideas. “So. A UC cruiser on a K-type mandate. Fine. A DSSA carrier we cannot name. An ages old beacon built in a hurry that says Guinevere ran into big trouble in the worst accent I have ever heard. And our cone points at a sector I cannot buy a permit for.”

“Why does a DSSA carrier drop a beacon and carry on as if it were just another normal day,” Captain Yuen asked the room at large. “Someone should be screaming. Yet DSSA says no knowledge.”

“Either the DSSA carrier was not DSSA,” Hermine said, “or someone has asked or paid very nicely for silence.”

“Or both,” Lya said. “The maths does not mind which of your politics you choose.”

Jasmina looked at the clean cone, then at the ugly satellite, then at the sealed case by her chair. The Quirium unit was quiet.

“We need a name,” she said. “If a carrier was in that pane and not on any DSSA ledger then someone filed it somewhere else. Hermine, what’s up?”

Hermine still looked uncomfortable.

“There is a person,” she said. “An associate who talks to me when I invite him to ‘94 Lavian Brandy. He calls himself Cal because he likes being difficult. He collects myths about early hyperspace work and calls them safety lectures. Last time we spoke he warned me off the northern pane and how it spooked early explorers. He called it the Umbra Sagittarii like he wanted the words to stick in my ears. The Archer’s Shadow. It sounded strange that he made that remark at that time.”

“He also called Deep Space Surveys a ‘little NGO’,” she added sourly.

“He knows something about this region?” Howard asked.

“Maybe, maybe not,” Hermine replied.

“Do you trust him?” Captain Yuen asked.

“I trust that he believes he is right,” Hermine said. “And that he answers questions with a different question unless you trap him in a corner.”

“So trap him,” Lya said, cheerfully unhelpful. “Rouse him with jam and judicious advice. Give him conundrums to guess.”

All the others turned their heads towards the TelePro in unusual simultaneity. 

“What?” Lya protested. “No one said scientists can’t be poets! We’re hunting a Snark here, aren’t we?”

Jasmina nodded once, irritation still written on her face. “Well, worth a shot, poetry or not. Ask your Cal. Tell him we have a dead cruiser’s whisper and a route that ends in a permit lock. If he wants to keep us out he can explain why to the authorities. Remind him I have a direct line to the Federation, Empire and the Alliance. That should be enough of a trap to motivate him.”

Hermine’s silence contained movement, the kind made by fingers calling in favours. “On it,” she said. “But I can’t promise.”

“I know,” Jasmina said.

Hermine turned to the captain. “In the meantime keep the fleet on the published scaffold. Survey Refinement Alpha continues. Quiet eyes on K-types along the cone. No heroics. If a DSSA carrier is out there under a different flag then it is either bait or a friend. I would prefer to know which before we say hello.”

“Understood,” the captain said. “I’ll work on something plausible with logistics.”

On the far wall the cone hung like a pale spear pointed into a map that refused to be helpful. Jasmina felt the seam in her bones again, the miss on fifteen that had followed them since Mars. Out here it sounded like something tapping at a locked door with more patience than she wanted to imagine.

Jasmina looked out at the K-type stars plot. The ghosts were learning to write. The missing carrier had to be the blank page ready for the words. Now she needed someone to tell her what was being written.

articles.title: Pirate Activity Surges as Security Forces Redeployed
articles.summary: Sharp rise in pirate activity across Imperial and Federal colonies as security forces redeploy to HIP 87621. Traders and miners report sustained harassment. IISS acknowledges 'temporary pressure' on border systems.
articles.player_impact: Pirate activity spikes in Imperial and Federal colonies due to security redeployment to HIP 87621. Increased interdictions and miner harassment. Bounty opportunities.
articles.modern_impact: Security vacuum created by superpower military concentration demonstrates the fragility of colonial defenses. Pirate groups learn to exploit great-power conflicts for territorial gain, a pattern likely to repeat whenever major forces are drawn into peripheral conflicts.
articles.body_full:
Local authorities across several Imperial and Federal colonies have confirmed a sharp rise in pirate activity, coinciding with the military confrontation surrounding the HIP 87621 enclave.
Traders report increased interdictions along previously stable shipping lanes, while independent miners have warned of sustained harassment at long-established extraction sites. System security offices acknowledge that patrol coverage has been reduced, citing the redeployment of forces toward strategic objectives elsewhere.
A spokesperson for the Imperial Internal Security Service commented that “temporary pressure” on border systems was inevitable while major forces remained on standby around HIP 87621. Federal officials echoed similar sentiments, stressing that order would be restored once current campaigns concluded.
Independent pilots have voiced growing frustration, describing a lack of response to distress calls and a noticeable absence of rapid-reaction forces in areas once considered low-risk. The Pilots’ Federation has urged authorities to address what they describe as a “security vacuum” before confidence is further eroded.
With no indication of an immediate drawdown in military commitments, analysts warn that pirate groups may continue exploiting stretched defences until normal patrol levels resume.

articles.title: All along the Watchtower
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: Near the Seldowitch Nebula in the Thuecheae MT-Q e5-8 System, Commander LilacLight discovers a drifting carrier-scale mass at the Praei-two permit boundary. Elaine Howard and Jacky Hew board the derelict prototype vessel with Halsey. They find GalCop-era hybrid drive technology, strange filaments, and nanite-compound residue that has partially consumed crew bodies. The ship's logs suggest an evacuation by T-9. Nadya Holdstock connects the find to a pattern of ancient technology.
articles.player_impact: The discovery of a derelict prototype carrier with dangerous nanite residue prompted immediate quarantine protocols and warned pilots away from the site, while raising questions about secret shipbuilding programs using obsolete technology.
articles.modern_impact: This chapter confirms that pre-Federation technology experiments continued into the modern era in secret, with catastrophic results—suggesting that the nanite compounds may be related to Guardian or GalCop meta-technology that modern science cannot safely replicate.
articles.body_full:
Thuecheae MT-Q e5-8 System, 3312 AD

The Seldowitch Nebula hung like a bruise in the darkness, a scatter of red along its rim where young stars bit through the dust. Distant World explorers swarmed the area. Mapping drones went out. Out here, there were dragons.

Mineral teams took polite bites of rings. The bulk synthesizers that kept the limpets coming were always hungry. Science kept its lists. Jasmina played her part on the briefings and then stepped off the stage, because behind the public cadence the flotilla had other work. And because Azalea scolded her to eat and sleep. On occasion.

Lya’s map, based on the corrupted cone and that ancient satellite’s broken voice, gave the search and rescue detachment a thread to follow. They slipped spin-wise and up between scheduled survey legs, flying quiet. The space around was remarkably unremarkable. Why were parts of the area locked down? And what did ‘Praei’ even mean? An illusion of normality was just about to insert itself into…

“Cold mass, carrier scale,” a certain Commander LilacLight radioed in from afar. From somewhere. “No transponder. No power. Drifting on a lazy vector toward the Praei-two plane. Looks like we're at the boundary of that permit lock. No in betweens.”

The image that came back filled the glass of one of the Odysseus’ holo-walls: A lone planet hung below a somewhat ordinary star. In its grasp… a carrier? But… not. Bigger along the spine than most, broad, modular, with parts strangely resembling the recent Squadron class carriers; but with odd bulges where docks should be. No callsign. No livery. No lights.

“Prototype,” Elaine Howard muttered. “I recognize some Brewer modules maybe. Someone built a secret and forgot to paint the name?”

“Locator team, passive scans only,” Hermine directed. “Don’t wake it up. No telling what the hell is going on here. Be careful out there, we’re moving in.”

---
Caution gave way to boredom, the carrier seemed utterly inert. Hermine eventually conceded they needed to find out more. She pulled up the duty roster: Elaine Howard and Hewley Jackman.

“Oh… this is going to be fun,” Hermine said, shaking her head in amusement and tapping in the summons.

Elaine arrived on the boarding bay already zipped into an old Alliance Scouting and Exploration Wing jacket, rank flashes still stitched where the regs say they belong. Four Purple Starburst ribbons glinted on the breast like knife-cuts that had learned to shine. Someone asked her once why she still wore it. “History,” she had said. That was that.

“Approach it,” Hermine said. “Passive scans first. If it sneezes, back out. We don’t know why this ship is here, or what it was doing…”

Jacky Hew, HewHew to his drinking friends, rolled a shoulder as the maintenance crew ambled past. “If you’d de-rate orbital cruise by a tenth you’d bleed less heat on approach,” he drawled.

“You will not preach orbitals in front of my people,” Elaine said, not looking at him. “You will hold a clean stack and you will not crash until after I’m finished with my ship.”

Hew grinned. “Copy that sir, Flight Major, sir!”

She didn’t correct him, just gritted her teeth. History.

“Just take Jasmina across, survey the ship, see if you can find out what was going on over there,” Hermine said. “We need some answers. Tell our Commanders to prep likewise. Second wave.”

Elaine looked at her, across at Jasmina, who gave a small nod. Elain then looked back to Jacky with a glare.

“Let’s go then, we’ve got a job to do.”

---
They went in through a maintenance lock that had jammed open. Jasmina was with them, despite their concerns. “It’s the Quirium,” she had insisted. Silent nods and no complaints. 

The inner skin of that carrier told a story of haste and bad choices. Bulkheads patched with plastisteel. Storage racks welded where designers never meant them. A tang in the air like hot plastic and stressed electronics.

“What a mess,” Jacky muttered.

“Lights to low,” Elaine ordered, the kind of tone that makes a panicked room breathe. “No touching anything that wants to be touched.”

They were twenty metres into the spine when the first filament lifted from the deck. The width of a finger, the length of a life, translucent and threaded with glitter like dust caught in a beam.

“What the fuck is that?” Jacky demanded.

“Hold it,” Elaine said. Everyone held still.

Jasmina tasted a metal tang in the air. The sealed Quirium Control Unit in the case at her hip shivered against her side as if remembering a rhythm she had tried to forget.

“Something?” Elaine asked, not taking her eyes off the slowly waving filament.

“It’s reacting,” Jasmina said. “Either the ship itself, or that thing…”

They eased past the filament, which didn’t further react to their presence.

They found the drive section two levels down. The chamber still smelled of tritium handling, an ozone tang mixed with machine oil, but the banks that should have held the fuel were empty. Converters along the aft bulkhead showed slag where heat had climbed beyond design and then stayed there. At the heart of it a gimballed cradle carried a lattice of gold mesh and dull ceramic wired to the reactor with an elegance that had no right to live beside angry welds.

“Hybrid rig,” Elaine breathed. “Primary tritium feed, secondary… I’ve not seen anything like this before...”

“I have, on a lone science station in the Sadr Region,” Jacky said, the smugness clear in his voice.

“And?” Elaine demanded.

He took his time, clicking his tongue and licking his lips audibly.

“Just say it,” Jasmina said.

“That’s pretty close to GalCop tech,” he replied. “There was this stuff called Quirium,” he nodded towards Jasmina and her device. “One geek out there thought he had it all together but blew himself up. I saw his crazy matrix once when I borrowed some synth materials from him.”

They stopped and listened.

“What? You think old Jacky and his yarn? I may be crazy but guess what.” He pointed to the gold lattice. “Looks like plasma coils. Pretty much like in Sadr. Old school. Not fuel lines. Some kind of control lattice. Like they meant to shape a field with Quirium the way old witch-drives did. But there’s no Quirium here. Nothing in tanks. Nothing in residue. They ran on tritium till the converters cooked. Then boom…”

Jasmina’s case thrummed like a trapped heart. She set it out on the deck plating. The throb rose, missed on fifteen, rose again. Filaments along the bulkhead turned their ghostly tips as if listening.

“OK… this is creeping me out,” Elaine said, soft and absolute, before pointing at Jasmina’s case. “Is that thing dangerous? We should get footage for Nadya Holdstock.”

“Not so far,” Jasmina said. “But it’s definitely reacting to these filaments. And yes, use your bodycams.”

The corridors were worse on the way back. The filaments had found friends. Sheets of the same glistening substance hung like wet banners between racks. Where they pooled they turned glossy and granular, a skin of polymer with a shimmer that made the eye slide away.

“What the actual fuck!” Elaine stammered.

They found the first body at a junction. Or what had been a body. The suit had slumped, then flowered into a framework of grey protrusions, struts and fingers that had no business being based on a human form. A faceplate peered from a web the way a seed looks out from a pomegranate.

Jacky took a scan.

“Nanite compounds,” he said, voice unusually serene and tight. “Not medical. Looks industrial. Partially decomposed… partially… disassociated and reformed into new chemicals.”

What had been an outstretched arm was now mangled, partially altered in form, looking almost like a badly designed mechanical grip manipulator.

“Do not touch,” Elaine snapped. She angled her camera and told herself she would not remember this in her sleep.

“What could do this?” Jasmina asked.

Jacky shook his head. “They were messing about with some weird shit onboard, that’s all I can tell you…”

They cleared the command level after an hour of cold caution. The primary bridge was dead. Consoles showed a last logon screen then garbled data. The secondary bridge still had power to a few spines, just enough for light. There were no more bodies, but in places there were patches of the grey substance sticking to walls and corridors. It was matt and featureless, eerie, but inert. They could see the remnants of suits, RemLok masks and uniforms embedded in it.

“Most of the crew didn’t get away,” Jasmina said, swallowing. “They’re still here…”

“Here,” Elaine said, jabbing at a console.

The logbook was incomplete. Earlier entries were neat, then hurried, then angry. The last entry was typed in a rush.

The line stopped as if the hand had been pulled away by someone rude to endings.

“Evac where?” Jasmina asked over Elaine’s shoulder. “Some did escape? Where did they go?”

“Flight deck,” Elaine said while downloading the logs. “If they launched that T-9, the answers would be down in the bay in the launch protocols.”

The bay had been purged. The interior was scorched and tarnished. Clamps showed marks where something big had slept then woken, burning out at full throttle and boost. The air smelled clean in a way the rest of the ship did not.

“Maybe they got out before the goo caught up with them?” Jacky asked.

“Maybe,” Elaine said.

Jasmina shivered. This wasn’t the answer, neither was it the question. But this grey goo was involved. She knew that for sure.

---
They pulled back to the Caspian following a thorough decontamination routine. Hermine took the lead with the patience of someone who likes plans more than surprises. The engineering teams were already pouring over the data from the log and the scans. Nadya Holdstock, their fuel wizard was present, too, her ponytail tucked away under her service cap as usual.

“We can leave it to drift and hope it meets a star,” Hermine said. “It’s a graveyard based on what you’ve discovered. DSSA doesn’t seem to care anyway.”

Jasmina nodded, unable to form words.

“Quirium…,” Jacky said ominously. “Converters burnt out. Tritium feed is repairable if we strip a tug. We can bring it to idle with enough rods. If you want…?”

“You and your Quirium. Another yarn tale?” Hermine shook her head.

“I don’t think we should touch it again,” she continued, eyeing Jasmina’s case as if it might answer back. “Whatever they were doing got out of control… same might happen to us. Last thing we need is some weird nanite epidemic spreading across the fleet. And actual Quirium fuel? In 3312? What does this even mean?”

At that point, Nadya Holdstock cleared her throat: ”Doctor Falayn’s fuel was lost long ago. But it was lost in the upheaval that was caused by the disintegration of GalCop. So we have a recurring pattern based on ancient tech, which may be more important than the fuel itself. It was a prototype and apparently failed dramatically. So we can’t use it.”

She looked at Jasmina: “But add to this your curious Quirium Control Unit from the depths of the Tionisla archives, the Fimbulthul’s GalCop deep space sensor array that was apparently ‘borrowed’ from the Sarasvati and the Faraway era satellite the DSSA carrier used as emergency comms beacon.”

“What are you implying?” Hermine asked.

“Nothing, just that there is a pattern of technology that today is poorly understood and exceedingly difficult to replicate.”

Elaine stood with the bagged log in her hand, jaw set. “Let’s focus. There is a Mayday and we’re still missing people in a T-9,“ she said. 

“We have no clue where they went,” Captain Yuen interrupted. “If that’s all you could pull from the logs, even with the current stellar density, it’s the proverbial haystack.“

“A science team left in a hurry and we don’t know where,” Elaine said. “But if they’re alive they’ll have answers. If they’re dead they might have logged something useful. This GalCop stuff is getting weirder and weirder and we need to get to the bottom of this.”

“And you’re ex Alliance,” Jacky laughed. “You bought them out, remember?”

“Ha, ha, ha, jackass!”

“Elaine is right,” Jasmina said. “We must either find them or ask around if they turned up somewhere. We’re in a better position for the latter at this point.”

Hermine nodded. “DSSA?”

“Yes. I feel they owe us some answers anyway.”

“Orders?” Elaine asked impatiently.

“Quarantine cordons everywhere,” Captain Yuen said. “Any reports of anything weird and we clamp down hard. Pull samples for Lya under burn boxes. Then more scanning.”

Jasmina looked at the dark shape on the main screen. A nameless carrier with a nameless hunger in its bones. The sealed Quirium unit at her hip ticked once.

“Send to the DSSA Council,” Hermine told comms. “Contact made with an unmarked carrier adrift near the Praei-two plane. Prototype drive with hybrid architecture. No power. No crew. Strange residue onboard. Quarantine in force. We’ll leave a warning beacon alongside advising visitors to give it a wide berth.”

“And the evac craft?” Elaine asked.

“Note an auxiliary craft is out there somewhere, probably a jury-rigged T-9,” Hermine said. She swallowed. “Tell them the truth: location and vector unknown. Not sure they made it, the logs mention an unstable reactor.”

Jasmina watched the preparations and the orders. There was a slight sense of relief, but also foreboding. A premonition. She was beginning to understand… but there was much more left to learn.

We’re on the right track… but where does it lead?

articles.title: Distant Worlds 3 Expedition Marks Major Milestones on Route
articles.summary: Distant Worlds 3 reports major milestones including Colonia regrouping, hazardous surface landing near white dwarf Spoihaae XE-X d2-9, Seldowitch Nebula surveys, and DSSA carrier discovery. Fleet bound for Beagle Point.
articles.player_impact: DW3 expedition milestones: cleared inhabited space, reached Colonia (WP1), 'Monde de la Mort' surface insertion, Seldowitch Nebula (WP2), Deep Space Support Array carrier discovery. On course for Beagle Point.
articles.modern_impact: Surface insertion at 'Monde de la Mort' establishes white-dwarf proximity landing as operationally feasible. DSSA carrier discovery expands known support infrastructure in deep space, potentially enabling longer-range independent expeditions.
articles.body_full:
The Distant Worlds 3 expedition has confirmed a series of key achievements as its diverse fleet continues toward an unexplored region of the galaxy.
Expedition control reported that the flotilla has successfully cleared inhabited space and completed its first major staging objective at Colonia, designated Waypoint One of the current route. Colonia served as the fleet’s primary logistics and regrouping hub before the start of extended deep-range operations.
While the fleet consolidated in the Colonia area, many independent commanders carried out a hazardous surface insertion on a lifeless rocky world informally dubbed the “Monde de la Mort” by pilots. The landing has been cited by organisers as one of the most technically demanding surface operations of the expedition so far due to its dangerously close orbit around the white dwarf star of Spoihaae XE-X d2-9.
The fleet has since reached Waypoint Two at the Seldowitch Nebula, formally catalogued as Thuecheae MT-Q e5-8, where large-scale stellar and planetary survey operations are currently underway.
While conducting extended exploration work in the surrounding volume of space, expedition search teams also identified a carrier believed to be associated with the Deep Space Support Array. The discovery has been formally logged and referred to relevant authorities for review.
With survey and logistics schedules within projected margins, organisers have confirmed that the fleet is now on course for its next historic objective: Beagle Point, the celebrated terminus of the original Distant Worlds expedition.
Elaine Howard, naval consultant for the expedition, stated:
“Operational progress remains strong. Commander participation, scientific output and fleet coordination have exceeded expectations. We anticipate arrival at Beagle Point on schedule, barring unforeseen navigational or stellar hazards.”
Further updates will be issued as the expedition advances deeper into uncharted space.
