articles.title: October Consortium Agreement Signals End to HIP 87621 Enclave Conflict
articles.summary: October Accords end HIP 87621 enclave conflict. October Consortium chairs neutrality between Imperial, Alliance and independent powers. Federation not represented. Lexi October secures interview series with Vox Galactica.
articles.player_impact: HIP 87621 conflict officially ends. October Consortium gains full custodianship via October Accords. Federation excluded (lost foothold). Radicoida research to be shared under Accord terms.
articles.modern_impact: Corporate custodianship of disputed territory sets a legal precedent for non-state actors mediating between superpowers. October Consortium's rise from tech investor to geopolitical broker demonstrates how exobiological discoveries can rapidly reshape power structures. Federation's exclusion may fuel future reclamation attempts.
articles.body_full:
An agreement has reportedly been reached between October Consortium and a coalition of the remaining Powers within the enclave, ending large-scale hostilities in the region.
The "October Accords” formally places HIP 87621 under the custodianship of October Consortium who will act as chair between the remaining enclave powers to ensure neutrality is maintained.
Under the terms, the corporation will also retain responsibility for system security and commercial rights, with authority to defend those interests if challenged.
The talks are also understood to have focused on shared scientific access to Radicoida unica and cooperation on research initiatives following the recent publication of promising genetic findings by Dr Casimir of the Holloway Bioscience Institute.
The coalition involved - an informal alignment of Imperial, Alliance and independent Power forces – had recently announced a non-aggression pact intended to prevent further escalation in the enclave.
Analysts suggest the arrangement had created space for diplomatic settlement rather than decisive military resolution, with no single power claiming majority control over the enclave.
Sources close to the recent discussions confirmed that the Federation was not represented, having lost its foothold in the enclave during the opening stages of the conflict. President Felicia Winters was unavailable for comment.
In the past months, the powers ejected from enclave conflict have increased their offensive activity within the core systems against the remaining enclave Powers. Analysts have concluded that a rapid diplomatic ending to the enclave conflict was required to allow redeployment of forces to defend against this aggression.
The rise of Lexi October and the growing influence of October Consortium since the discovery of Radicoida unica has not gone unnoticed, however, and Vox Galactica has confirmed that an interview with the Consortium’s reclusive chief executive has been secured for an upcoming feature series.

articles.title: First Lattice, Part 1
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: Back at Phoenix Base on Meene, Ram Tah and Uwe Toramund analyze data from the derelict carrier via telepresence with the DW3 flotilla. Ermitage reveals that the Guinevere is an Eridanus-class cruiser with cryo-stasis crew rotation, rarely used because freelance explorers make it unnecessary. Ram Tah presents a radical theory: the phenomena are connected through "hypertemporal space"—a lattice where time has zero value and events can be entangled across vast distances. He suggests the Guardians' AI-based communication network may still exist in witch-space, and that something is trying to contact Halsey through the Quirium Control Unit.
articles.player_impact: The hypertemporal theory implies that Guardian-derived technology and witch-space anomalies may be interconnected across the galaxy, affecting any pilot using FTL travel or Guardian-enhanced equipment.
articles.modern_impact: This chapter reframes the entire narrative from isolated incidents to a unified theoretical framework: witch-space as a hypertemporal lattice where Guardian AI, GalCop technology, and modern events are entangled—a concept with profound implications for interstellar civilization.
articles.body_full:
Meene, 3312 AD

They were back at their computers, displays and charts. They even had to repurpose an adjacent storage room for more displays and memory banks. All the leads, analyses and models ate more computing power than a Cartographics terminal after one of the Distant Worlds expeditions.

Engineer Ram Tah scratched his head, folding his big brows into the ‘V’ his assistants knew as a sign of deep concern. To his side, his senior assistant Uwe Toramund made some final entries in his personal holofac.

“I need the data from Jaques laid over the data we received yesterday from that carrier. The goo stuff. Then put their flight itinerary to the right and highlight where the expedition did their surveys. Only pick the bigger ones.”

Turning to Toramund, he continued: “Set up telepresence to both send and receive, Tor. Audio only, otherwise it’ll burn through our capacitors.” 

Half an hour later all the displays were set neatly in a mostly helpful arrangement and the base’s TelePro buzzed happily until the receiver sprang to interstellar life. Expectations were high as this was the first telepresence comms attempt after the flotilla’s FTL arrays had been adjusted.

“DW3 ExCom, do you copy?” Ram asked into the void. “This is Meene Base on Echo Comms. Please acknowledge.”

There was an awful lot of noise. Not really static, it was more like a geiger counter complaining about a radiation shower. Then suddenly a beep.

“Yes, we copy. Halsey here and with me are Miss Delarue from DSS and Elaine Howard. We have no request for a visual from you, why do you want audio only?”

“Because the data you sent eats our memory banks and bandwidth. I could buy more memory from the Feds or the Empire but I think it’s a bad idea right now. So we’re somewhat limited. We also can’t get Lya into this, she is still occupied with setting up shop in Orion.”

“It’s working?”

“Well, last I heard she had a heart attack.”

“What?! Because of a few light years?”

“No, one of her instruments lost its calibration or something.”

The head shaking was audible from this side of the galaxy.

“Still,” Ram continued. “Did you manage to get a big picture over there already? We have some ideas we can share but Tor and I also rely on what you think this is all about. After all, you are the visionary here, Madam Envoy. Literally.”

“Vaguely,” Halsey conceded. “And call me Jasmina please. I’m not hosting an Embassy reception. Jaques set us on the trail. He said he witnessed a number of equipment failures inside the station itself and near its perimeter. We had a look around and confirmed it was real, although we couldn’t figure out the reasons. But you already know this.”

“It’s a wonder that station still survives out there, but Jaques’ not only good at serving drinks. When they started to get serious about that patch of space he helped install the very first generation of hardware over there. I reckon no one else would have sensed what was going on there sooner than him.”

“He still clicks his mouth when he gets agitated. He also said the events started to happen when a certain UniCart cruiser came through and uploaded some explo data.”

“The Guinevere? The ship you asked us here to verify?”

“Yes. Did you come up with something?”

“Not much,” a voice echoed from behind the Engineer and his assistant. An old man stepped forward, neat grey suit and blue tinted glasses.

“Interesting. Do I hear a Mister Ermitage?” 

He didn’t bother to answer that.

“I don’t put much trust in the Pilots’ Federation and their cartographers. You know that. Too much bias and too many stock options involved. Still, there are a few things of note. They don’t have many Eridanus-class cruisers because they are specifically designed and equipped for extended deep space survey missions. 

But neither the PF nor UniCart use them very often. They require secondary crews in cryo stasis for such long operations. Too unpopular, too costly and with armies of freelance explorers exposing themselves to the dangers of deep space willingly, such assignments just aren’t necessary anymore. Buying their data is cheaper.”

“But they still had one out there,” came Jasmina’s voice. “And they must have found something. Seems they came across some Guardian beacons while at it and had nothing better to do than get some juicy fighter blueprints?”

“That’s our guess, yes. At least according to what Jaques said. But without flight or cargo manifests we’re not getting anywhere. UniCart won’t tell us.”

“DSSA must have caught the flu then when they met near Rendezvous Point.”

The old man cleared his throat. “Halsey, I realise Miss Delarue has approached my dearest contact on that matter.”

There was a brief pause. “Yes?”

“He won’t tell you anything about it. Don’t waste your breath. His specialty is making obfuscated remarks. He is usually correct in what he says but attunes his wording to what’s expected of him.”

“He knows a lot about GalCop technology.”

“He does. He used to work for them. Well, in a way at least.”

Silence. 

“Are you still there?” 

“Who is this guy?”

The old man’s face darkened. “Believe it or not, he’s still on our side at this point.”

“And I’d never thought I’d say that,” he pensively added. 

“At this point? What on Earth have you set us on here?” came the answer. It was Hermine Delarue’s voice, angry across a thousand light years. “Do you have an idea how dark it’s out here? And I mean in terms of puzzling this all together. Seriously, what were you thinking?”

“Jasmina, you are absolutely on to something,” Ram Tah interrupted. “You need to get to the bottom of this.”

“But why? Why do I even carry this Quirium unit? Is it the Holy Grail to a mythical Avalon? You said you have ideas, models and stuff. Pray tell me, what is going on with your fancy numbers, Ram?”

“Very well,” he said. “First, it’s vital you try and see everything connected, despite distances that seem vast and times that are forgotten.”

“Too lyrical, Ram. What do you mean?”

The Engineer eyed Ermitage and Toramund, then continued: “The gist is, nobody has a clue how Hyperspace — hyperspatial cosmology — really works or if that term really describes what’s going on. Despite its discovery a thousand years ago, we can build engines on a hunch that enable transdimensional portal inception but actual research into the matter hit a snag long ago.”

“Until recently,” Toramund added. “Actually, the data you provided us with made it possible to refine a number of theories that had been shelved. Too outlandish at that time and… too non-conformist for major league industrial donors.”

“You mean frameshift tech?”

“Not precisely. Early Einsteinian relativity assumes space and time were inseparably entwined and on the same spacetime lattice. It’s a crude theory but it has worked for a long time. But some think they are separable and that hyperspace, or more precisely hypertemporal space, is actually the not so theoretical result of this split.”

“I don’t understand that at all.”

“It’s pretty new to us,” the Engineer said. “Ask Lya. She is one of the few who already have a degree in Temporal Theory. The ‘Temps’ say hypertemporal space exists everywhere at once. In their equations, time has a value of zero, meaning a hypothetical point B in space can be reached from point A instantaneously. Or events that are entangled, for lack of a better term. That’s why we think all the spectacle you encountered is connected, but in a way we don’t yet understand.”

“You say it’s new to us. You think someone has actually developed this hypertemporal tech in secret?” Jasmina asked, more or less rhetorically.

“No. Not remotely possible. At least not by human standards and that’s where it gets interesting and why I said us.”

“You mean I’m not going to say it’s aliens but it’s the aliens?”

“Sarcastic but pretty accurate. We correlated all the data from the Guardian sites last November with the events that occurred near that timestamp. Interestingly, you collapsed in Congress under duress of your first returning vision when our dear explorers started scrutinizing the obelisks. And there were a few thousand light years in between so our theories and hopes it’s a local phenomenon are void — literally.”

“I know what you’re aiming at but that doesn’t explain why that Tionisla marvel resonates whenever something happens or is about to happen.”

“I think it does. The lattice on which these events happen over vast distances, and more or less simultaneously, is remarkably similar to what we think we know about Guardian communication, which was heavily reliant on the use of their version of artificial intelligence — if they actually regarded it as such.”

“And?”

“And your Reuben Hale in Tionisla alluded that your Quirium Control Unit held an at least semi-autonomous assistance firmware at some point, meant to regulate the complex process of Quirium injection, while preventing the process from becoming uppity.”   

“And you think the unit responds to what you call a hyper… hyper… Hell, I can’t even remember what it was! That lattice, because someone wants to control it? I remember Hale saying some GalCop projects ‘forgot themselves’. I thought that was a joke in Delaney’s direction for being…”

“Uppity?”

“Yeah.”

“For what it’s worth, at this time I don’t think your Quirium Control Unit responds to something. I think it’s the other way round. Something tries to make contact with both you and the unit. And this something, in not so scientifical terms, is literally all over the place and at the same time. It resides in hypertemporal space — witch-space. All indications lead to this conclusion.”

“The visions…”

“Exactly. You said on Mars you felt a fabric under tension and voices warning you about something in witch-space. You called them Caretakers, which implies a sentience with a moral compass and an understanding of community, and that they were afraid. We know of one species out there whose society reflected these concepts. Apparently, those weren’t metaphors, Jasmina.”

“The Guardians.”

“Yes.”

“And the degenerate compounds we found on the DSSA carrier and later the evacuated T-9? They were here, not in witch-space. Another thing forgetting it existed until summoned from the depths of the Archer’s Shadow”?

At this point you could hear rolling eyes on the bridge of one of the distant carriers.

“We don’t know yet. We simply don’t. We sadly have no physical sample so have to rely on remote methods. Preliminary analysis suggests the materials were broken down on a molecular level, including organic matter. It’s probably not radiation but rather age related decomposition. Decay; natural decay but in materials that either don’t have one or one that’s exceedingly slow. But that doesn’t explain the structures you refer to as ‘nano goo’ and it doesn’t explain why the T-9 wasn’t wholly consumed.”

“And the crew?”

“Whatever is at work here, it’s probably easier to break down organic matter than plastisteel or proto-alloys. You really found some nightmare stuff there, Jasmina.” 

“We need to make sure no one finds it, not in a lifetime. Not ever. We are going to have DSSA destroy it.”

“Probably the best course of action,” the Engineer said.

“Still, if what you say is true,” Jasmina added, “the technology is out there somewhere waiting to be found. I know when GalCop collapsed a lot of their research was sold off to the highest bidder by the remaining opportunists. Yes, some accuse the Alliance and especially the Turners but it’s foolish to assume there weren’t others. Ermitage, I think you would agree with my completely unfounded statement?”

Another proof sarcasm could be transmitted over vast distances without loss of aim and context.

“It’s very, very unfounded, Halsey. People love you for your casual statements that have filled the dirt files of your political adversaries.”

“It’s the skeletons we make along the way.”

“Jasmina, you do politics,” the Engineer interrupted again. “You say tech but this thing probably isn’t even working technology. I doubt that material decay is on purpose. If you want to invent a word, call it meta-tech. But I don’t need to tell you whoever gets a hold on this would be swimming in trillions upon trillions of credits by next Friday.”

“I doubt the Guardians or my Quirium Unit are interested in trillions of credits.”

“Probably not but I have an idea. I need to find out something, although it may be increasingly difficult to make unseen moves.”

“What do you mean?”

“Well, you agreed to share your findings with all the committees in the world, remember?”

“Yes?”

Ram Tah looked at Ermitage, eyebrows raised. Stepping forward again, he answered the obvious concern: “The last dossiers we filed were answered with some very detailed questionnaires, kindly asking for more information. Ambassador Delaney and I try to stall them, bury them with nothingburgers. But it won’t last forever. When political politeness fails, you suddenly become a person of interest and narratives begin to shift.”

The Engineer chimed in again. “We’re pretty safe here, rest assured. I still have people who owe me. However, before scrutiny increases I need to corroborate something. Something you probably shouldn’t concern yourself with. It’s going to be here in the Bubble anyway so just continue your jaunt and keep us informed.”

“You’re not going to do anything stupid, Ram, are you?”

“Me? No. I have an army of ghosts for that.”

articles.title: Core Dynamics Unveils Kestrel Fighter
articles.summary: Core Dynamics unveils the Kestrel, a pure combat fighter with speed, agility, and three Mk II large hardpoints. Supercharged FSD is a first for a small craft. Limited release at Duamta.
articles.player_impact: Kestrel early release at Polyakov Station, Duamta. Limited availability initially. Combat trial missions within 15ly. Size 5 thrusters + supercharged FSD on small frame.
articles.modern_impact: Supercharged FSD on a small combat craft represents a design philosophy shift toward speed-over-versatility. Mk II Plasma Shock Accelerator compatibility suggests Core Dynamics is standardizing next-generation weapon platforms that may see adoption across Federal and independent naval forces.
articles.body_full:
Core Dynamics has announced the limited release of the Kestrel, a new small combat ship engineered exclusively for high-intensity engagements.
Designed as a pure combat fighter, the Kestrel prioritises speed, agility and striking power over versatility. Its compact frame, Size 5 thrusters and high-speed manoeuvrability make it particularly effective in close-quarters combat, interception duties and rapid strike operations. Engineers have also confirmed the ship will be fitted with supercharged Frame Shift Drives, a first for such a small craft.
A Core Dynamics senior test pilot stated:
“The Kestrel was built with a singular purpose: to win fights. Its handling characteristics and acceleration allow experienced pilots to outmanoeuvre much larger vessels, while the three Mk II large combat hardpoints, which can be fitted with the new Mk II Plasma Shock Accelerator, ensures it delivers decisive force when it counts.”
Early reports indicate that, in capable hands, the Kestrel can challenge medium and even large multi-role ships, with elite combat pilots pushing the design to its operational limits.
To test the new Kestrel’s combat capabilities, Core Dynamics has called for interested independent pilots to sign up at Polyakov Station in the Duamta system before accepting any Combat mission types from any Mission Board within a 15ly radius.
The Kestrel is available now as an early-release purchase and will later transition to wider shipyard availability.

articles.title: First Lattice, Part 2
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: At Phoenix Base, an AI Relic from an illicit courier transport breaches Ram Tah's workshop security and attempts to rewrite his matter synthesizer. In an emergency telepresence with DW3, Ram Tah reveals his investigation: AI Relics from GalCop-era transports are being smuggled near Shinrarta Dezhra. He tested one near Jackson's Lighthouse neutron star, where it began reorganizing matter on a nearby Adder. Lya explains that hypertemporal space is easier to access near hyperdense masses. Ram Tah distributes a firmware patch to help DW3 pilots detect frequency outbursts.
articles.player_impact: DW3 pilots received a firmware patch to detect anomalous frequency outbursts in their surroundings, particularly near neutron stars and white dwarfs where the witch-space entity appears to bleed through most strongly.
articles.modern_impact: This chapter confirms that GalCop-era AI Relics still exist and are actively dangerous—capable of hijacking modern systems and reorganizing matter. The smuggling network near Shinrarta Dezhra suggests powerful interests are collecting and trading this forbidden technology.
articles.body_full:
Meene, 3312 AD

ALERT! WORKSHOP SECURITY BREACHED! 
LOCKDOWN PROCEDURES IN PLACE! STANDBY FOR RESET… … …

“What the fuck!” Engineer Ram Tah screamed across the workshop comms system. “It tries to insert itself into the system. Tor, lock down prio one and two systems. Do it now!”

Looking through the plastisteel window of his workshop, Ram stared at the experiment he and Uwe had been setting up for two days: Embedded within what must have been hundreds of metres of cables and encased in a reinforced ceramic shell, a ribbed anthracite block, not larger than a conference suitcase, hung suspended in a magnetic field tube. 

There was no sign of activity whatsoever. And still that thing had sprung to a life of its own once it got its ‘incentive’.

Visibly alerted and perplexed, Uwe ran his fingers over the keyboard of not one, but three terminals. Red lights blinking here and there, interrupted by the occasional yellow and green. Subsequently a number of displays on the holoprojector wall went dark.

“Boss, I isolated life support and all external comms, broadband and FTL. Base integrity, landing pad force fields are intact. Up- and Download server isolated, base data seems secured.”

He looked up. “What is that?” 

Looking at the experiment again, the Engineer’s face showed raw bewilderment. He started to type a few sequences into a keyboard of his own, lining Trimex code row after row until finally hitting enter. Real programming. It was old school but he liked it that way. Kept things simple.

“I ran a system trace. The unit activated when we ran the frequency models. It then analyzed the workshop framework and got to work. But it’s not even interested in comms, operations or power. Wow! It’s… it’s trying to rewrite the matter synthesizer.”

“The what?! Shall I isolate?”

With his usual big ‘V’ brows Ram Tah hesitated for a moment, his face shifting from panic to fascination. “The matter synthesizer, Tor. Of all things. You remember our expedition friends mentioning they found decomposed matter? There is a purpose at work here, likely a very old one. What did radiocarbon say again?”

Uwe glanced briefly at one of the smaller workshop displays. “Extremely lower range so not older than 300 years.”  

“Boss!” he added nervously. “Shall I isolate? It’s compromising the workshop.”

“No. Shut down remaining priority one and two systems. Also, no docking permits and no customers. Tell them we’re under audit or something. And lay the synthesizer matrices on screen one.”

“Under audit? Are we?”

“Well, in a way I guess. That thing is starting to peek around.” He smiled his ‘I found something interesting’ smile, then he turned to his keyboard again. “Now, now. Let’s see what you’re up to.”

---
Telepresence. One of the marvels of the 34th century, but it had its limits. While it was possible to create a holo facsimile and talk face to face in this way, the extreme distance to the DW3 flotilla put a strain on the system each time they met. After all, all the signals still had to travel through hyperspace so there was a considerable delay and sometimes signal loss. So they had agreed to mostly use audio only.

‘They’ were Jasmina Halsey and Hermine Delarue from the DW3 “Odysseus” Flag Carrier, Astronomer Lya ter Holt from around Orion (hopefully) and Ram Tah from Meene in the Bubble.

The Engineer had called for an emergency meeting and he was just giving them the brief. 

“Remember a few days ago I said I needed to corroborate a few things,” he said. “I know I kept you in the dark but I had my reasons. Turns out they were not unfounded.”

“I need a bit more than that,” Jasmina interrupted. “There are people running around asking a lot of questions since we scrubbed that DSSA Carrier and found their evac ship. Even seasoned explorers get agitated when they feel they need to dump a half dissolved carrier crew and a vague cargo of something into a godforsaken crater in the middle of nowhere.”

“I know. But I have some answers. So hear me out first. We can then discuss later.”

“Very well.” 

“So it goes like this: Every once in a while an unremarkable courier transport with a very unusual cargo pops up near Shin Dez. No one quite knows where they come from and their allegiance callsigns are usually fake. But if you have friends with friends there, you’ll know.”

“Know what?”

“Know when they are underway. And as it happens, I have friends with friends.”

“Your army of ghosts?”

“Precisely.

“So what did they find out?” Hermine Delarue demanded. “I hope it all was worth it and that your hush hush didn’t link us to anything.”

“Rest easy. What we did is what we call an ‘isolated incident’.”

“Well, if they are transports, what do they transport then?” Lya asked

“Salvage mostly. Trinkets, personal effects of broken ships, the odd escape pod… But it’s a clever ruse. Most of these transports are decoys but some of them transport small, elusive technological marvels from ages past. They are indeed classified as AI Relics.”

“AI Relics?”

“Yes. Again no one knows. If you stop these ships they usually self-destruct and the crews, if alive at all, seem to have lost their memories.”

“This is getting wilder by the minute.”

“There is more,” the Engineer said. “These items are old, probably somewhere in the 250 years range, and if I recall you said that Dr. Reuben Hale from Tionisla said AI research wasn’t banned back then.”

“Yeah, GalCop. It’s always them in some way.”

“So while my ghosts chased down some of these relics I had the time and analysed the FSD mass telemetry you sent from your World of Death and the sector pattern from your Hunting of the Snark.”

“The Snark?”

“An incredibly ancient poem,” Lya interrupted cheerfully. “It was my idea! I love it. It’s about maps and beavers and searching for all kinds of absurd stuff.”

“Yeah, it all makes sense now…” a flabbergasted Hermine could be heard across the galaxy.

“It’s fascinating,” Ram continued. “You remember the Guardian ruins last November? Instead of using their million year old frequencies, they suddenly adopted a singular frequency in the picohertz range, source unknown. So we recorded the event.

Now, when you did your mass jumps at the World of Death there was a slight amplification in the exact same frequency range. And it’s interesting because the amplification wasn’t caused by your jumps per se but by that white dwarf. And that measurement was only possible because a good amount of your pilots mass jumped in direct vicinity of that dwarf. So you could say the dwarf helped catapult your ships on a teeny-weeny scale.”

There was an audible sigh. “Massive FSD engagements have often been speculated to create undesirable side effects in spacetime,” a weary Jasmina Halsey could be heard.

“That’s from the Federal Astronomical Journal!” Lya cheered. 

“Yeah, but picohertz is a bitch,” Ram spat. “After all, it's pretty close to gravitational waves. You need really dense matter. And had the distances been greater and hadn’t Lya been able to inject some of her ‘Temp’ equations with time being zero and whatnot, I probably wouldn’t have been able to detect them at all. But we now know where to look and I’m now able to run accelerated simulations so I can track them more easily.”

“So?” came Jasmina’s question.

“So? I had a hunch.”

“Oh, I guess this is going to be fun.”

“Well, sort of. After those AI Relics tried to usurp my lab…”

“They did WHAT?”

“Yeah, long story short, I hooked up one of those relics to my workshop where I usually fiddle around with Guardian based technology.”

“Are you fucking mental?” Hermine exploded.

“No, I’m Ram Tah. I need to keep my engineering weirdo reputation. So if you please let me finish: One of these relics tried to inject itself into my hardware. We managed to isolate and study it for a while. It didn’t try to usurp my base but it was very interested in my mass synthesizer. It began reprogramming the matrices.”

“But how is that possible?”

“I think because of an ancient inbuilt purpose. So I had another hunch.”

Sigh.

“I isolated the relic in a stasis unit and attuned it to the picohertz frequency we now can simulate and had it flown over to Jackson’s Lighthouse — a neutron star not so far away. A few friends then parked an old Adder right next to the relic.”

“Ooh! That’s so super smart of you, Ram,” Lya interrupted. “At the moment time is a constant in all equations and cannot fall below zero. If it could I would probably not date that Astrochemist on campus seven years ago. Come to think of it, time travel and if-clauses don’t really like each other. I have to write that down somewhere.”

“Lya, what’s your point?”

“Well… Umm… In a nutshell it means hypertemporal space is easier to cross into or out of when you are close to a hyperdense mass. Theoretically. It’s classic relativity with a few perks of my own. A bit like Albert ter Holt. Or Amanda Einstein. Or whatever. 

There is a lot of ‘hyper’ involved and those equations look more like ancient hieroglyphs,” she continued her cheerful rambling. “However, those new Caspians and their superduper-supercharges are the next best thing coming close. But they still can only extend jump ranges and not reduce hypertemporal transit time.”

“So what were the results at Jackson’s?” Jasmina asked.

“As I expected. When we deactivated the stasis pods the AI Relic started to get agitated. It tried to take over the Adder, drives and navigation first. At the same time we measured a spike in picohertz to the power of two hundred. It then started — and you’re gonna love this! — to reorganise the ship’s matter. Drives first, then hull, the computer, shipboard systems… Seems familiar?”

“Nanites?”

“No, not strictly. The polymers are deconstructed, reorganized and then consume other materials. There is purpose and function at work but after some time the newly formed matter just… decomposes. Decays. Loses its structure. We talked about that. I have never seen anything like it but maybe that’s why this AI thing was very interested in my mass synthesizer.”

“Ram, we have thousands of explorers out here. I need options and an action plan. We’re about to leave the Abyss and enter more frequently travelled space again. What’s your assumption?” 

“Jasmina,” the Engineer said gravely. “Simply speaking, whatever this is, it’s feeding on gravity waves, bleeds through, uses Guardian technology as a carrier and is able to reorganize matter on a ship-size scale.”

“Bleeds through what?” Hermine asked.

“Your witch-space,” Lya said happily. “Your friend lives in your witch-space. You’ve been talking about this since the beginning. Your voices, you always say they are not really here. Plus, it’s the only way Ram’s new friend can influence so many things on a galactic scale.”

After a pause she added: “If we ‘Temps’ as you call us are right, hyperspace exists in a zero time continuum. For maths it’s not a problem to handle three more dimensions. It’s just that FSD technology is transient and doesn’t let us stay there. But whoever or whatever actually does has all the options of an Altair Five-Card Draw.”

“This is what it meant back then,” Jasmina mused. “In those visions on Mars, and later in the Tionisla archives. Project Caretaker, the voices, the Missing. It’s Guardian and it was a plea for help.”

“Yes, we established that as a strong possibility. But not only that,” Ram added. “There must be another entity involved, and if it rides the Guardians as a carrier it probably has access to their remains and their resources. Take the obelisks for example. It supplanted their frequencies.”

“Something is broken in witch-space. That’s what it told me in my very first vision on Mars. Something wants to bleed out but it can’t. Not yet.” Jasmina mused. “We need to make sure we understand more. We need a new angle.”

“Yeah, good you have me,” Ram said. “I improvised a firmware patch, sending it to you now for fleet distribution. Tell your pilots to upload it to their sensor suite.”

“You think they will do it?”

“Why not? They have been downloading modified embedded firmwares, security firmware patches, cat media and settlement defense plans for years now.

Based on our models, it should help them detect frequency outbursts in their surroundings. Tell them to scan a few neutron stars to see if it works properly. Then I would suggest quietly doing a bit of sightseeing along your way. Look for wake irregularities when you mass jump, especially near neutron stars or white dwarfs. Neutrons preferably, since their distortion fields are much more dense.”

“You think that’ll work?”

“You’re on an expedition. Stop here and there, take a few selfies. Just look as if you belonged there, shouldn’t be that much trouble.”

“It’s been a while since I felt I belonged somewhere but I guess I can manage. ExComm out.”

Over telepresence Lya and Ram Tah exchanged some last concerns, shrugged unseen shoulders and terminated their connection.

articles.summary: Vox Galactica profile of Lexi October reveals her rise from tech investor to dominant corporate power. Key milestones: Supratech rescue (3305), Joker's Deck incident (3307), and current control of HIP 87621 through October Accords.
articles.player_impact: Deep lore article on Lexi October. Reveals her history: rescued Supratech in 3305, hosted Joker's Deck (Winking Cat theft), and controls HIP 87621/Radicoida via October Accords.
articles.modern_impact: Reveals October Consortium's hidden history: Supratech rescue (3305), Joker's Deck incident (3307), and Artemis suit manufacturing. Lexi October's comment about 'reminding everyone who manufactures the Artemis suits' implies military supply-chain leverage over major powers, a strategic advantage that may be exercised in future negotiations.
articles.body_full:
Vox Galactica business analyst Marlon Royce has published a feature piece on October Consortium CEO Lexi October:
“Few figures in the Core Systems command as much quiet influence as Lexi October in recent months.”
“Known for identifying promising technologies before rivals recognise their value, October has built a portfolio spanning advanced engineering, pharmaceuticals and personal tech. Exobiological research is the next challenge.”
“Her hands-on approach came to light in 3305, when the Consortium rescued struggling tech firm Supratech. The investment stabilised the company after poor sales of its Torc computing system and enabled further development of products such as the Artemis exploration suit.”
“October’s reputation for discretion was reinforced in 3307 when she hosted an exclusive gathering for the secretive Joker's Deck, attended by political and corporate elites including Zachary Rackham and Scorpio DeVorrow. The event made headlines after master thief Winking Cat stole a priceless artefact.”
“October declined to discuss the incident in detail, stating ‘Security failures are lessons. The important thing is how quickly you adapt.’”
“More recently, however, corporate scrutiny has focused on the Consortium’s long-standing permit control over the HIP 87621 system, where the rare organism Radicoida unica may hold the key to a new range of market-leading pharmaceuticals.”
“October confirmed her position on the recent October Accords and a coalition partnership with several Powers. ‘The agreement will ensure Radicoida research is accelerated and shared fairly, with October Consortium retaining oversight. I’m looking forward to seeing the results of this cooperation.’”
“When pressed as to how October managed to negotiate the Accords with several Powers at once, she simply smiled at me, stating ‘When you put decades of research on the table it’s a big incentive. That, and reminding everyone who manufactures the Artemis suits.’”
“It'll be interesting to see what the future holds for October.”

articles.title: Echo Chamber
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: In the Abyss Region near Beagle Point, the DW3 flotilla experiences the psychological toll of extreme deep space travel. Alessia Verdi observes the growing unease among pilots. Jasmina Halsey notes the Quirium Control Unit has been silent since the carrier discovery—troubling her more than its previous activity. Medical staff document cases of Deep Space Dissociation Syndrome: pilots hearing voices in sensor noise, engineers experiencing disorientation, crew having persistent dream-fragments. Jacky Hew remarks that modern carrier jumps feel too smooth, as if "something else is doing the work." The unit trembles once before returning to silence.
articles.player_impact: Deep space pilots on long expeditions face documented psychological effects from extreme isolation, with reported symptoms including auditory hallucinations, disorientation, and persistent dream-like states that blur the line between external anomaly and internal stress.
articles.modern_impact: This chapter explores the psychological reality of deep space exploration, connecting historical generation ship tragedies to modern "space madness"—while suggesting the Quirium unit's silence may be as significant as its previous activity.
articles.body_full:
Abyss Region, 3312 AD

The galaxy did not end with a wall.

It thinned.

That was the only honest word for it. The density of stars that had once crowded every canopy began to loosen, their patient abundance giving way to widening gaps. Navigation plots grew sparse. Fuel calculations grew cautious. Plotting computers buzzed with impotence. The great spiral that had held humanity’s attention for centuries no longer surrounded the Distant Worlds flotilla. It lay behind them now, like the memory of a crowded room after the door had closed.

Beagle point had been reached. It was pretty much the edge, looking past that was looking into pitch darkness with no end.

Behind lay everything else.

The convoy stretched across supercruise in a slow, deliberate procession, thousands of ships moving with the careful restraint of travellers who understood, perhaps too late, how far from home they had come. Carrier wakes braided faintly in the void, their geometry precise and fragile, while smaller vessels darted between them like fish sheltering beneath larger shadows.

From the cockpit of her Caspian explorer, the USS Ceilidh, Alessia Verdi watched the procession with the distant detachment of someone who had long ago learned to distrust the romance of exploration.

She had joined the expedition late, catching one of the last fleet carrier departures from the Bubble as it burned its way outward toward Colonia and beyond. She had told no one why. There had been no point. Pilots rarely asked questions whose answers they did not want.

Now she leaned against the canopy rail, arms folded, eyes half-lidded, watching the convoy with the clinical patience of a veteran soldier observing new recruits discover their limits.

She knew they were beginning to feel it. All of them.

Not fear, exactly.

Something quieter.

Something older.

Fatigue did not arrive suddenly in deep space. It accumulated, imperceptibly at first. Sleep cycles drifted. Concentration wavered. Small mistakes appeared, corrected quickly and quietly, but not forgotten. Conversations repeated themselves. Pilots found themselves staring at instrument panels without remembering what they had meant to check.

In the carrier concourses and mess halls, speculation had replaced celebration.

The discovery of the nameless carrier drifting near the Praei permit boundary had left a bruise on the expedition’s collective psyche, and the still unknown mission of the Guinevere deepened it into something harder to ignore. The official bulletins remained calm, precise and reassuring, but the gaps between those words had begun to speak more loudly than the words themselves.

Alessia had heard the questions. They were good questions.

Why K-type stars? Why neutron stars now? Why had a prototype carrier been built around a hybrid Quirium architecture that no one officially knew how to manufacture? Why had it been empty? Why had it been alive? Secret comms back to engineers in the bubble, about what?

The questions circulated in bars and corridors and private comm channels, accumulating like static.

She didn’t volunteer her own speculation. It was too early for that. Experience had taught her that answers arrived when they chose to, not when they were demanded.

But she knew the symptoms well enough. Deep space missions always went like this.

The space madness was starting to show.

---
Jasmina felt it too.

Not in her mind.

In her bones.

She stood alone in the quiet of her quarters, the sealed Quirium Control Unit resting on the table before her like an object that had not yet decided whether it was a tool or a warning.

It had been silent since the discovery of the carrier. That silence troubled her more than its voice ever had.

She had come to recognise its cadence, its strange, hesitant attempts at communication, the subtle misalignment in reality that accompanied its moments of awareness. Now it lay inert, its gold mesh and ceramic planes absorbing the soft cabin lighting without response.

She wondered if it was listening. Or waiting. Or hiding.

Beyond the bulkheads, the convoy moved steadily towards the next waypoint, each jump bringing them closer to the edge of mapped space and further into regions where charts ended and extrapolation began.

She had reviewed the medical reports earlier that cycle. The medical staff were playing it down, but she knew they were worried. Deep Space Dissociation Syndrome.

The name sounded clinical, manageable, safe. The reality was none of those things.

Pilots reported hearing voices buried in sensor noise. Engineers described moments of disorientation while performing routine diagnostics. Service crew reported dreams that persisted into waking, fragments of conversations and places that vanished when examined directly.

Individually, each report could be dismissed. Together, they formed a pattern.

Human cognition had evolved beneath skies that provided context. Horizons. Reference points. Boundaries. Out here, those boundaries no longer existed.

The mind adapted poorly to infinity. Generation ships had discovered that long ago. Their silent hulls still drifted in forgotten systems, monuments to optimism and endurance and the quiet, inevitable erosion of certainty.

Jasmina wondered if those early crews had felt it too. The sense of being observed by something that wasn’t using eyes.

---
In Odysseus' primary bar, the mood had shifted from celebration to endurance.

Pilots gathered out of habit rather than enthusiasm, drawn by gravity that had nothing to do with mass.

Jacky Hew held court near the observation viewport, his voice carrying the rough confidence of someone who had spent too long trusting his instincts to stop now.

“Carrier jumps,” he was saying, gesturing vaguely toward the stars, “they’re different. Smoother. Cleaner. Back in my day, when I scouted the neutron highway, you felt every transition. Your ship complained. Your bones complained. This new tech… it’s like something else is doing the work for you.”

Someone laughed nervously.

“You saying you miss the old days?”

Jacky grinned, but the expression didn’t quite reach his eyes.

“I’m saying,” he replied, “that when things get easier, you stop asking why. When you see the void start staring back at you, that’s the time to pop the pills.”

Alessia, having docked aboard, listened from her usual corner, nursing a drink she had no intention of finishing.

She recognised the tone around her. It was familiar enough from her adventures in the Formidine Rift. She shivered.

Not fear. Not yet. But… unease.

The first cracks were appearing.

---
Jasmina returned to the bridge and stood at the observation rail and watched the slow procession of ships preparing for the next jump cycle. Thousands of independent pilots, scientists, soldiers and dreamers, all suspended at the edge of known space.

They had come seeking discovery. They had found questions instead.

Behind her, unnoticed, the Quirium Control Unit trembled once.

A single missed beat.

Then silence.

Jasmina did not turn.

She was already listening.

And somewhere beyond the reach of charts and permits and human certainty, something else was listening too.

articles.summary: At DW3 Expedition Command in the Veils Region, Lya and Ram Tah present their lattice model: a filament network connecting ultra-dense masses, mass jump locations, and anomalies across the galaxy—including Colonia, Guardian ruins, Tionisla, and permit-locked sectors. Halsey activates the Fimbulthul's GalCop sensor array and detects a "singing" anomaly near the Veil's Ember supernova remnant. Expedition Commanders discover a wrecked RimLiner Galactic Anaconda from the 2900s—one of "The Missing"—with the same hull disintegration pattern. Halsey takes the Quest to investigate but disappears without a high wake signature. Nadya Holdstock secretly reports to Ermitage that the Caretaker Protocol may still be active.
articles.player_impact: Expedition pilots contributed scanning data that revealed a galaxy-wide lattice network, leading to the discovery of a centuries-old Missing vessel and raising concerns about an active Caretaker Protocol affecting deep space navigation.
articles.modern_impact: The chapter confirms the lattice is real and measurable, connecting anomalies across the galaxy. Halsey's disappearance without conventional FTL signature suggests access to non-standard hyperspace transit—possibly related to the Quirium unit or Caretaker technology.
articles.body_full:
DW3 Expedition Command, Veils Region, 3312 AD

The data didn’t just trickle in. It nearly overloaded Fimbulthul’s already vast databanks and barely left any processing power for modelling the intake into a cohesive something. The thousand or so neutron stars that had been scanned by expedition Commanders over the last week provided a much needed insight into what they were actually tracking out here. 

In the one or two days that followed the galaxy spanning telepresence team had managed to puzzle a few pieces together. At one time they even included Jaques back in Colonia. And although most of the time he had limited himself to an “ah yes, that one” or a “this is probably as accurate as it gets”, his knowledge of old technologies on the other hand had come in more than handy. 

So with all that data Lya and Ram Tah had been able to come up with a simulation that could best be described as a fine network or lattice of filaments connecting ultra dense masses. And what was perplexing: This network also connected to locations with extreme hyperspace entry telemetry — their so-called mass jumps — and places that for lack of a better term could only be described as anomalies — points of interest that didn’t fit into one of the prior categories. Purpose unknown or unconfirmed. It was a gigantic spider’s web laid onto the Milky Way. It was absurd to not think a hidden purpose lay behind all this. Caretakers, architects…

Interestingly, Colonia was one of these anomalies. The Guardian ruins in the Synuefe and Wregoe sectors near the Bubble were others. And Tionisla of all places. There were a few more and some of them were quite concerning. Some were very concerning. Some of them were permit locked. 

“There!” a holographic Lya pointed her finger right into the equally holographic display they were all sharing. “The models don’t lie. This… this lattice is real. I mean in the sense that it exists and can be measured. And on top of that it shows we ‘Temps’ may have a point with our highly unconventional zero time continuum thingie after all.”

Across the telepresence projector and quite a few light years between them she shot Ram Tah a flirtatious smile. “Nice work, Mister Engineer. When I’m back home I need to juggle a few more dimensions in my comfortable maths equations and see where that gets us.”

Ram’s holographic brows formed their characteristic ‘V’.

“Aye and thanks. But you are home, aren’t you? This is just… telepresence?”

“Oh I know! I mean when DW3 is over. I need to publish this once the models are tried and tested. Don’t worry, Ram, you’ll be credited.”

At that point Jasmina Halsey interrupted. 

“Not so fast with our galactic horses. We need to put it all to work here. We have unfinished business with our friends in witch-space and some AI that tries to reconfigure matter for reasons unknown. This is not for academic publication but for fleet communication. Any guesses? We need to tell our 8,000 Commanders something.”

“Why?” Lya asked.

Jasmina shifted from one foot to the other, a rare sign of nervosity.

“When people don’t have something to do, the same people start to talk. Just ask Jacky. There are a number of mess hall discussions around any number of topics. Gossip mostly, but some of these talks always circle around the things we saw and what we found out here. The inexplicable bits. And when I say ‘out here’ I mean in this remoteness of space. People get anxious when they can’t place events or find explanations for the things they see. You can try and divert their attention with hydroponic gardens and a few stratum techtonicas but ultimately they will start making connections themselves, some of them nearly always turning out to be unhealthy.”

“So what do you suggest?” the Engineer asked.

“I suggest finally making good use of that GalCop wizardry on the Fimbulthul. They took elaborate efforts to install, nay, jury-rigg these sensor array relics onto the carrier and they are supposed to help in deep space surveys. Well, we are as deep in deep space as it gets and this Mister Ermitage seemed quite certain it would be of good use when the time comes. And I think that time has finally come.”

“We don’t know if it’s even working,” Ram mused. “Ermitage was pretty vague about its capabilities — let alone its origin.”

“Well,” Jasmina said, “let’s see if it works at all. And if it doesn’t we can still pull the plug.”

“That’s what I thought back in my workshop, too, not so long ago. It’s easier to contain a planetside base than a flotilla in a non accessible area of cold vacuum.”

“I agree. Turning one of our carriers into a flying listening post isn’t what I had in mind when I joined. But we have tonnes of unfinished, raw data and limited options. The array, however old and odd it may seem, was meant to augment our surveys and that’s what we’re going to use it for now.”

“Jasmina,” Lya said. “That’s all and well but can I recommend to sever all non essential connections to our other science operations for the time being? Like Ram, I don’t fully trust this technology no matter how sophisticated it may seem. With a stressing on ‘seem’.”

“Noted,” was all Jasmina had to say to this.

---
First it was an anomaly, a shiver in their filament, but it was pointing somewhere promising: a neutron star in a bright supernova remnant. Because of its location and colors earlier explorers had dubbed it the Veil’s Ember. It was one of the more prominent locations in this remote area of the Milky Way so the team was surprised to have it show up on the diagrams at all.

They had managed to give the lattice a visual form in all their simulations. Right now it was like a thin fabric laid on a liquid surface that was the galaxy. It came complete with ripples and eddies and around the Ember remnant the holoprojector showed a blurred eddie, maybe some fifty light years in diameter. It was… science beautified.

“There,” Lya said. “We found it roughly two hours ago. It’s a strong signal and it’s singing in perfect harmony with your lattice signature and with what we would call a density event. Mathematically speaking it’s a perfect equation. We can’t pinpoint its exact location, though, the model isn’t refined enough.” 

“Singing?” Jasmina frowned

“A curious metaphor, I know.”

“No, not at all. I sometimes wake up in the middle of the night thinking I hear a choir out there singing in witch-space. All these visions and voices, they more and more blend into a melody of sorts. It’s strange but it always… soothes me.”

“You mentioned a lot of people see or hear eerie stuff in your flotilla. That’s why I don’t like space travelling, I guess. There are just too many unknown variables floating around and some of them now seem to have a life and voice of their own.”

“So that GalCop array works?” Jasmina abruptly asked, looking left.

At her side, Nadya Holdstock nodded. She absently brushed a strain of her blonde hair aside and cleared her throat.

“Yes, it does, at least according to the specifications from Mister Ermitage. He gave some instructions on how to online the array to the Fimbulthul’s sensor dishes and so far there have been no incidents of note.”

“Of note?” Jasmina shot.

Nadya just looked at her, her face expressionless.

“So he gave you the specs in advance?”

“Of course.”

“What aren’t you telling me then? You and Ermitage? You worked together putting the logistics in place back at DW3 HQ. You know him personally, do you?”

“You know that already so why the question?”

“How long? And what are you even to him? Just a coincidental Quirium tech? Where does all this secret knowledge come from? Is he in league with this ‘Cal’ guy?”

“And I ask: Does it matter here and now? He apparently knows what he is doing and although I doubt he could have foreseen the exact odds we are facing, his insight into old technology has served this expedition well.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“But this is my answer to your question. And yes, he is what you call in league but not in the sense you think he is. He is also in league with you, Halsey; and with Delarue and in fact with most of the hirings for this endeavour. Now, do you want us to find out more about this singing anomaly or do you want to persist in futile questions?”

“How dare you…”

“Guys!” Lya pleaded over a thousand light years. “We have a space anomaly and Jasmina, you want to tell 8,000 people what to do. Guess it’s not the time to tell them to go explore family trees, no?”

Jasmina hesitated for a good moment, apparently wrestling with her composure. One final glare at Nadya, but finally responsibility won over.

“Good. Let’s go sightseeing then. Tell Jacky to take out his Krait. I want him around when we find out more. Elaine will stay with me on the Odysseus, coordinating things from here.” 

---
The anomaly turned from a shiver in the fabric into a solid wreckage; another one. Intrepid Commanders found it near the Ember in a somewhat unremarkable system. Jacky Hew was still out with them. It was unusual the wreckage had lain hidden for so long but the multitude of stellar bodies in the system along with some probable earlier explorer’s space boredom may have been parts of the reason. 

The wreckage itself was huge, bigger than the hapless T-9 they found near the Seldowitch Nebula a month ago. It was an Anaconda-class vessel, half buried in the moon’s regolith, half broken with parts strewn around. It wasn’t long before SRV teams were on site, trying to uncover the ship’s fate.

Meanwhile, back at the carrier Jasmina and Hermine Delarue had quickly assembled their usual debrief team, including Nadya Holdstock and also Captain Yuen from the Halsey’s Quest. The Caspian was already on pre-flight checks.

“Right, people,” Jasmina began the debriefing. “I asked Nadya and Jacky to go over the footage and data we received from the wreckage. Jacky, you’re still out there, you need to keep them on a leash for the time being and don’t let them do anything stupid. You know, SRV jumping over the ‘Conda, paintballing themselves or something similarly ridiculous.”

“Righto, Ridiculousness is one of my major talents, my Lady.”

“Yeah, right,” Hermine mused.

“Okay, team. There are several Commanders out there now waiting for some feedback so let’s throw together what we have. Nadya?”

With a stern expression Jasmina looked at the technician. She clearly hadn’t forgotten the barbs traded earlier.

“The wreckage is interesting,” Nadya stated matter-of-factly. “I was able to analyse most of the data explorers have gathered and also parts of the hull itself.”

“Not bad for a fuel tech, eh?” Jacky Hew jabbed over telepresence from his Krait.

Nadya just shot him a glare through the projector that immediately shut him up, which was rare enough.

“Right, ahem…” was all he could mutter.

“It is an Anaconda, yes,” she continued. “And it bears the same hull disintegration we have seen in the DSSA carrier and its evacuated T-9. That much is certain but that is not all.”

“What do you mean?” Hermine asked.

“Despite its sorry condition there are some incongruities I could identify. The model is missing some of the characteristic features of a modern Faulcon deLacy production line. Instead, what once must have been a cargo hydraulics module was manufactured by BTS — Beerbaum and ThruSpace. It is a very peculiar model used only in the original production lines.”

“Never heard of them.”

“BTS was contracted by the original Anaconda manufacturer, RimLiner Galactic. RimLiner in turn was bought up by Faulcon Manspace in the early 2900s, before they even merged with deLacy Shipworks. This means our Anaconda is a very old model. Probably first or second generation. A barely visible ‘RLG’ marking on the bow corroborates this.”

Silence.  

“There is more,” Nadya added. “If it is a RimLiner model this would imply it must have had a Quirium hyperdrive with a probable maximum range of fourteen light years. Maybe twenty-eight before refueling. Sadly, the wreck’s drive section disintegrated. However, for all we know there was no means to manufacture Quirium outside of inhabited space. This means it is extremely unlikely this ship could have made it here on its own.”

“Oh, this get’s better and better,” Hermine sighed.

“A few weeks ago I would have said it’s absurd,” Jasmina conceded. “And yet, with all that we have met and seen along the way and the findings our brilliant minds came up with I’ll now put it in the realm of the possible.”

They looked at her.

“What? I mean I now believe in visions and hear ghosts talking and singing to me. This is just another day at the office for me now.”

“I guess we just found one of those expeditions that the Federal archives call the Missing,” Hermine said.

“In any case,” Jasmina continued, “I need to get a closer look myself. Captain Yuen, get the Quest ready and I think I will carry my little Quirium friend with me.”

She then turned to Delarue: “You have the flotilla. Take them along the expedition itinerary. I’m taking the Quest and scout ahead. I need to see a few things for myself. Or rather feel. I’ve been chained to the ready rooms for too long. We’ll meet up at the next waypoint. Until then, have the TeleTeam find out what they can.”

“Yessir!” Whether in earnest or in friendly mockery, DSS Operations Executive Hermine Delarue stood at attention and saluted, leaving an even more confused and head shaking Jasmina storm off the bridge. 

---
“What do you mean, she’s gone?” Elaine Howard turned to Flight Lieutenant Moyers of Odysseus. “Of course she’s gone. She registered her FSD jump and flight plan a minute ago. What’s the problem?”

“Ma’am, I don’t know if it’s a problem at all.”

“Then why bother?”

“Sorry ma’am, maybe I should have been more precise. Miss Halsey’s ship left sensor range accordingly but… there is no high wake. ”

“What? Check your scanners, Moyers.”

“I just did, ma’am. Last known position at body 1a. Flight plan initiated at 03:47. Sensors still indicate a mass lock but I don’t have anything on scan.”

“Send out some Commanders. Tell them to sniff around, only in nicer terms.”

Eight minutes and thirty-two seconds later they had their reports: No ship, no mass lock and most importantly no high wake. But the very same location their “Lattice Signature” firmware picked up a massive… something. It was like a dissolving tissue in water, a fabric that had been there but now wasn’t. Something… fading? Or maybe closing?

“A portal collapse?” Elaine mused, looking at the data. “It’s similar to a carrier jump pattern. No conventional FSD spool-up and no high wake.” 

“But not even a Caspian can do that,” Moyers said.

“No. But maybe something else can.” 

Or someone… she thought. 

“Inform the fleet, ma’am?”

“Good heavens, no! This is opsec now, Moyers. Top team and Senior Carrier Command only. The last thing we need now is people getting agitated over Halsey disappearing again. There’ll be a bushfire of tinfoil, visions, spooky witch-space, Thargoids, Architects and whatnot. We had that already ten years ago. Just tell them Halsey is out in her Quest, scouting ahead.”

“Very well, ma’am. I’ll log the event as Alpha-1 confidential.”

---
In her Asp Explorer, the Inscrutable Sanctuary, Nadya entered a series of commands into the comms console. She was a jump out from the Ember, knowing the neutron star could have jeopardized the precision alignment of the Sanctuary’s FTL dish. After having entered a final code sequence the small holofac came to life, projecting the image on an old man. 

“Mir, earlier than agreed on. What is it?”

“We located the wreckage of an Anaconda out here in the Veils. There is credible proof it’s a RimLiner Galactic model from the 2900s. Corroded hull, missing drive section. There is a solid pattern now, John.”

“Interesting, so the Caretaker Protocol wasn’t shut down after all. I need to have a word with him about that. Did Halsey already send her weekly debrief to the Bubble?”

“No, she is scouting ahead in her Caspian. She is confused and I assume she wants closure or confirmation on her loose ends. She took the Q-Unit with her.”

“Good. Her debrief mustn’t go out. We have  enough trouble covering up Ram Tah’s interesting experiment. The chance of leaks is too great. See to it, Child.”

“Understood.”

And with that she terminated the short exchange and leaned back in her pilot seat, marvelling at the beauty of the Ember.

articles.title: Taking Care of Caretakers
articles.author: Andrew Gaspurr
articles.summary: John Ermitage and Cal meet in secret aboard an old converted mining platform in the Tianve system. They debate the ethical implications of rapid deep-space expansion, the dangers of unchecked technological progress, and the mysterious Caretaker Protocol — an apparent remnant of GalCop-era AI research that may be manipulating hyperspace and matter. Cal admits ignorance of the protocol but warns that humanity is overextending itself. John reveals that the Distant Worlds expedition has gathered evidence of hyperspace bleeding into normal space near superdense masses, and that old comms from missing ships have been received through FTL channels.
articles.player_impact: The discussion reveals that the expedition uncovered evidence of an ancient or artificial intelligence manipulating hyperspace — information that could affect every pilot travelling through witch-space. Cal's warnings about overextension mirror concerns many independent explorers have about unchecked expansion into the galactic North.
articles.modern_impact: The article frames the Caretaker Protocol as a potentially existential mystery linking GalCop, Guardian technology, and modern hyperspace anomalies. Cal's reluctance to engage and John's determination to investigate suggest a fundamental disagreement about humanity's readiness to confront what lies beyond the frontier.
articles.body_full:
Tianve, 3312 AD

There was an out-of-the-way jewel in the Tianve system. It was an old mining platform at the fringes of the rings of Tianve 9, an otherwise unremarkable icy body in the outer system. The platform had been converted into an observation and entertainment complex by the Tianveian Tourist Board, the TTB.

It was in one of these conference suites the two old men met. While John, the fossil with the blue tinted glasses, sat in one of the yellow lounge sofas, his 'old acquaintance' Cal stood in front of the wall sized crystal window, a tumbler with Lavian Brandy in his hand. He had his back turned to John and was seemingly taking in the glittering, prismatic ring spectacle.

"Fantastic isn't it?" he said to himself. "Tianve of all places. I nearly forgot this place existed. Did you know back in the day people thought there was a pulsar in this system? Those clever TTB marketing bastards."

He then turned to John. "An excellent example of mass manipulation. When the hype was in full swing and the liners were underway they sold all their shares and were never seen again. They knew it would take the liners two weeks to get here. Enough time to liquidate a company and look for greener pastures."

With his legs crossed, John had also chanced a few looks outside. Tianve was still part of the Old Worlds, that ancient conclave of systems that had mostly been settled by early independent souls and mom-and-pop expeditions rather than by industrial heavy weights.

He looked at Cal and just nodded.

"Well," Cal continued. "I understand why you chose this place for a meeting. At least around here nobody wonders about a Lanner flying around with all its parts intact."

"I knew you'd like it," came the eventual retort. "Where heist crimes meet nostalgia."

"Well, if those are the criteria we should have met on Founders World. Or even on Jameson Memorial. The place for the Elite's elite. More fitting, don't you think?"

"John Ermitage," he added. "Ermitage, really? I never took you for a hermit. When the dust settled all these years ago, I always imagined you flying around the galaxy with your newly found friends and freedom, seeing all the places you couldn't in life. Well… in your former life I mean."

"Only it wasn't dust that settled after these actions but ashes," John replied calmly. "Ashes that were the fallout from your shortsightedness."

"The Powers that were begged to differ on quite a few things. But we've been there, John. Done that, got the proverbial T-Shirt. Why have you asked for this meeting? To see me staring at a neutron star that never existed?"

"No, Cal. It's not about nostalgia and it's not about T-Shirts. But funnily it may have something to do with neutron stars and also with things that never existed."

He cocked his head. "I mean, you're the obvious expert on things that never existed, aren't you?"

"No, I'm the expert on making things vanish, John. There's a slight difference. But here we are again, two dinosaurs trading barbs as usual. You can't let go of our old enmity and I fully accept you never will. I was prepared to never see you again. And when you nonetheless came to me last year I told you from the beginning your 'window for cooperation' was a bad idea. Our interests rarely did align."

With that John got up from his couch and walked the few steps towards the crystal window. It was true, it was a magnificent view, pulsar or not.

"Well," he said. "If that's the case then, fine. Still, you seem very enthused to speak with Miss Delarue every once in a while. Maybe the window for cooperation was meant to be not with me but with someone else in the first place?"

He looked at Cal, eyebrows raised — slightly.

"Yes, I enjoy her. She was a good pick. She has a sharp mind and a more general, strategic level of morality that doesn't get in the way all the time because of some minor nuisance. There is still a steep learning curve, to be sure, if you want to play the big game. Having her butt heads with the Dog Star nutters may prove to be a challenge."

"And you?" John asked. "Are you a challenge?"

"Ah," he waved off the question. "It's fine. She asked me a lot about space travel and the galactic North. She obviously doesn't know how space exploration on a big organisational scale worked back then."

"I wonder what you might have told her."

"No, you don't, because you already know. In any case, I did the honest thing and warned her. Sometimes quite bluntly, sometimes with some metaphorical help. I told her humanity should have no business up there."

He paused for a moment. "It… didn't really deter her, I think. Quite the opposite, actually. She seemed especially intrigued by my Umbra Sagittarii reference. Enticed even. There is a very honest curiosity about her, the kind of curiosity that can get you into trouble at times… She reminds me of someone…"

"Yeah, that Umbra of yours never gets old, does it? Space yarn tales."

"You may believe me or not but I was earnest when I warned her. There are regions we shouldn't be in. Not yet. We are over extending. But we keep pushing boundary after boundary just because of 'The Frontier'."

He waved towards the scenery outside the crystal window with his brandy tumbler.

"You know very well, where it got us last time, my friend."

"And who makes the decision when it's time? You say you make things vanish but at the end of the day you deny humanity their path to the stars. And while you may find that phrase amusing it's the truth. Not trying to expand our experience and broaden our horizon means stagnation. You say it's dangerous because you think someone will discover something you guardians of the galaxy can't control."

"Guardians of the galaxy, heh! That's even funnier than all the things they said about Halsey's hallucinations. Or about Patreus' saber rattling how the Pleiades had always been ours to take."

"And no, John. It's more complicated than that and I'm sorry to break it to you but it's about responsibility. It's dangerous in a socio-evolutionary way. Bluntly put, we are progressing too quickly because we think technology and our own grandiose ingenuity allow us; because we can. Then again, governments aren't responsible. They are hasty and greedy, thinking in years or decades at most. Just look at all those lifeless, deserted outposts the Trailblazer Initiative left after a few never-heard-of shell companies started to throw credits around. Is there coherence? No. They are scattering their resources where fancy takes them."

"It's always refreshing seeing you talk about ethics and responsibility," John said. "And I disagree. Human advancement was always driven by exploration and expansion. You can see how the governments' attempts to regulate space exploration have clearly failed. You can't regulate what you can't control."

"I understand the allure but we're not talking about a trek to Oregon or even an outpost chain to the Pleiades. We are talking about space we won't be able to socially and economically curate for a very long time. Our fernweh enthusiasts are now on the verge of colonising the Lagoon Nebula. And for what I ask? Because they have been there and found it a nice place for taking selfies."

"Humanity is squandering resources that are desperately needed elsewhere," Cal finished.

"There are precedents," John said. "Take the Alliance for example. When their technological breakthroughs allowed it, they not only revolutionised space travel but it also ushered in a new era of small scale exploration not seen since the days of GalCop. The return of the mom-and-pop expeditions so to say."

"Argent knew what she was doing and she had acquired a huge stash of GalCop technology. And it only got her to the Corona Australis. But there never was a serious colonisation effort after and people are still searching for her missing Quest ship."

"And Mic Turner? He went to the Pleiades."

Cal smiled again, this time out of pity. "I'm not playing your mind games. I'm too old for that nonsense. And however enlightening it is to discuss galactic matters and humanity's place in all this with you, you once more didn't answer my simple question why you asked for this meeting."

"Very well then. Over the last several months the Distant Worlds expedition has acquired a staggering amount of factual data that hyperspace is somehow bleeding into our known space."

"Factual?" Cal interrupted.

"Yes. It seems especially prevalent close to superdense masses and massive FSD events. Their data suggests a possibly misguided intelligence is behind all this and yes, for the time being they ruled out the Thargoids. It seems to be attuned in some way both to ancient GalCop and Guardian technology and through some presumably old programming seeks to manipulate these for its own unknown gains. There have been a number of crude but corroborating references in the Tionisla archives that mention a 'Caretaker Protocol'."

He looked at Cal. "Ever heard of that before?"

"Caretaker Protocol? That's an interesting name, especially given you say that protocol is apparently not taking care at all."

"You mean you don't know anything about it?"

"I don't, John, as absurd as it may sound to you. I dabbled in a lot of things and know of other things that most people don't. But I'm not omniscient."

"Not anymore at least," he added wryly.

"Halsey said in Tionisla they told her the name came from an old GalCop project report. It must have had something to do with research into machine intelligence meant to control Quirium based FTL drive injections. Coincidentally, ten years ago, Halsey spoke about caretakers in her visions as well."

"It sounds like a very GalCop thing to do, asking a machine to please make FTL work for them. People were fed up with Faraway Jumps and riding high on all kinds of technological wizardry. But again, I don't know anything about caretakers. Yes, research into AI may have been a big thing but after a few catastrophic failures with recycling and environmental control and a few deaths, people decided it was a PR minefield and not worth the money. So they abolished most of it."

"Still, there must be something. You say recycling? They discovered several wrecks in your Archer's Shadow, some of them very old. Every one of them showed signs of matter manipulation on a molecular level. The last hull they found apparently was a RimLiner Anaconda. It can't have gotten there on its own."

"And this is your Caretaker Protocol? A thinking, teleporting recycler gone rogue?"

"I don't know, Cal. That's why I asked for this meeting. To ask you. You of all people still breathing are one of the rare specimens I can ask and expect to get an earnest and reasonable answer; one that isn't always a hundred per cent true but I can accept that."

Cal seemed to consider it all for a few moments and finally leaned against the crystal window. For a moment it looked as if he was falling into the void behind him. He sighed.

"Quirium is a lost case, John. You know that. GalCop collapsed under financial duress and scrutiny, economical and military donors far and wide pulled their cash, Sirius wanted the cake but came too late to the table. And Falayn vanished. Case closed."

"Not closed. We both know some of GalCop survived. People, places, assets… experiments maybe. You mentioned Meredith yourself and we know there were others at the proverbial table, including your 'employers'."

Cal weighed his head. "Maybe, John. But again, nothing of the sort. The governments saw their chance to forbid dabbling into AI after their own research efforts faltered. They didn't want others to succeed where they hadn't. The result was one of the very rare occasions where I would say they were right about it."

"There is something at work here," John mused. "A remnant of something. Not only in the galactic North. An associate of mine linked several puzzle pieces together in an experiment not long ago and was able to reproduce here what has happened tens of thousands of light years away."

"Yes, I know, it was this Ram Tah guy. The Wheel are starting to wonder where all their AI relics went. Soon they'll start looking, I'm afraid. However, it still doesn't explain why hyperspace is involved. And why your something is bleeding into our space."

"Communication?"

"How?"

"We use FTL comms ourselves and we know the Guardians did on a much larger scale. Whatever is out there allegedly uses — or rather usurps — their channels, so to speak. But it all seems to result in a jumble. We have heard distorted comms from ships that went missing ages ago. It's almost as if hyperspace was capable of storing all these bits and pieces."

"Well, guess what now, John! You're the one who had the brilliant idea to 'borrow' the sensor array of the Sarasvati, an old GalCop listening post. See the irony here? A listening post doing its job by listening and reporting? What were you thinking that old gizmo was going to do? Read the Galnet news to you?"

"We certainly didn't anticipate receiving comms messages from the Tau Ceti colonisation, the Birthright Wars, the Republic of Achenar or some other event hundreds of years ago."

"Seriously, why do you think people think witch-space is spooky and malign?"

"What if it's not witch-space that is malign but rather what may be residing inside?"

"I'll leave that to your speculating friends out there. And if your brilliant astronomer is right and hyperspace is indeed a zero time medium, information being contained there indefinitely isn't that far fetched. Maybe we're just lacking the correct receiver at the moment. I mean, look at how the cosmic background radiation was dicovered and later led to early astronomical breakthroughs."

"Like I said earlier," he mused. "Sometimes we are just not meant to have the technology for the next step. It's called the progress trap. After a period of rapid advancement and increasing social and economic complexity, any civilisation needs a revolutionary technological breakthrough in order to advance further. If they don't achieve it they will eventually vanish in a self-destructive struggle over resources. Again, I leave the interpretation to you and your friends."

"This doesn't sound like the man who thought he had the tools to play god."

"Because I never was that man, John. None of us were. For all your bitterness and your theories on caretaking, we were probably the next best analogy."

"And you're still doing it now?"

"Yes, oddly. However, there isn't much I can do right now. Your expedition is thousands of light years away, your little coterie of devotees is fractured, your senator is dead and the Wheel keeps turning, to borrow a phrase. And I told Delarue everything I could about 'ye olden days'. For what it's worth, she asked me to keep tabs on some potential backstabbers here in our very civilised space. You know, the usual suspects who want to cash in on a quick political win. But they are all freaking out about blue gardens now."

"Blue gardens?" John asked

"Yes, a Radicoida specimen. They are bioluminescent, hence the 'blue' pun. A very promising find. They are also a minor interest of mine."

"You don't have minor interests, Cal. That's why I called for this meeting."
